EntertainmentTab.title: Why brazen museum thefts keep happening nearly a year after Louvre heist
EntertainmentTab.text:
When thieves broke into a French museum earlier this week and stole four paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir, worth millions of euros, not everyone was surprised.

Just last month, the European policing agency (Europol) had warned that museum thefts across Europe were growing increasingly brazen.

And just days before the Renoir heist, internationally known art detective Arthur Brand predicted to the BBC that more high-profile burglaries were likely - particularly in the wake of the successful robbery at the Louvre in Paris last October.

The audacious crime in one of the world's most famous museums stunned France, and the stolen jewellery worth €88m (£75m) has still not been recovered, nearly a year on.

"We will see more of this," says Brand, "because if you are able to hit the Louvre, thieves all around the world are watching that, thinking, 'Wow' - and then they think, 'Don't we have a local museum with gold and silver?'".

Within hours of the Louvre burglary, thieves had raided coins from a smaller museum in France. Since then, criminals have stolen a diamond necklace in Vienna, Bronze Age artefacts in Spain, and art from two Italian museums - and that's only what the BBC has written about.

The heist at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer is the latest, and detectives are still working to track down the remaining multi-million-pound paintings - two of which were quickly recovered after thieves dropped them in the museum garden.

Europol tells the BBC the number of museum theft cases reported to them across Europe began to increase about two years ago.

Its recent report says both the methods and targets of thefts are changing - with a rise in more forceful tactics, and, as in the Louvre case, a focus on high-value items such as precious metals and gemstones.

Both Brand and Ibrahim Bulut, a museum security expert from a Belgian security consulting firm, believe many thefts that followed the Louvre burglary are copycats.

"Every museum in the world is stressing now," Brand says. "In every museum there have been meetings with the security officer or with the police."

Museums are vulnerable and easy to burgle, Brand says, compared with well-secured jewellery shops and banks - which these days hold less cash.

Directors historically "never have enough money for security" or prefer to spend it on the next exhibition, and museums are often housed in old buildings that are difficult to protect, he adds.

For example, the Denis Diderot Maison des Lumières (House of Enlightenment) - burgled hours after the Louvre - is housed in two 18th-Century mansions in Langres.

"We therefore have to reconcile modern security requirements with the need to preserve historic buildings and comply with France's heritage regulations," local mayor Théo Caviezel explains.

Museums are also open public spaces that have less access control and perpetrators can come in as visitors, says Kumar Sokka, CEO of Acre Security which works with some museums in Europe.

And even if a museum is secured well, thieves could still come in armed, Brand says, adding that it would be impractical to put police in galleries.

Many of these burglaries are over in minutes and the thieves have long gone by the time police show up - the Renoir case happened within five minutes.

Heists used to depend on deception, but burglaries are now becoming increasingly violent, Europol's report last month, external points out. Offenders are using tools such as sledgehammers, axes, crowbars and, in some instances, explosives, to get inside.

In the Louvre, the thieves used a mechanical lift to gain access, cut through the window with power tools and then threatened guards, who left, before forcing their way inside displays and grabbing the jewels. In the Renoir case, the perpetrators used an electric knife to cut through a fence before sawing through structures holding the paintings' frames in place.

The increased aggression creates new security concerns.

"An armed incident during opening hours, like the one we experienced, creates a situation in which the immediate priority is to keep our audience and staff safe," says Lilli Hollein, the director of the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) in Vienna, which was burgled last month.

What is being stolen is also changing. While paintings are still taken, they're harder to sell, so about 10 years ago, thieves began shifting to goods that are easier to get rid of, Brand says.

Now precious metals, gemstones, and culturally significant artefacts including Chinese porcelain are increasingly targeted, according to Europol's report.

"Precious metals can be easily melted down, leaving no trace for law enforcement, and facilitating illicit sales during the fencing process," it says. "Precious stones in jewellery, on the other hand, can be easily removed and sold further."

Meanwhile, Chinese porcelain is likely to be easily sold on the art market because of high demand, Europol says.

After a theft, police generally have between four and six days to catch the thieves, according to Brand, who works with investigators by calling informants and receiving tips from the public or even ex-partners of perpetrators.

But while suspects may be arrested, jewels or precious metals might not be found - such as with the Louvre case.

On the other hand, Brand believes the Renoir paintings stolen this week - two of which were dropped by the thieves on their way out - "will probably be recovered" because "no one will want to buy" them and "it is likely, then, that the thieves have no idea what to do with them".

Christopher A Marinello, the boss of Art Recovery International that recovers stolen art, says only 5-10% of stolen art is ever recovered, making thefts from small museums like this week's "extra painful".

Tuesday's heist is another example of "Europe's museums under siege", he adds.

Brand says a delay could be building an extra, heavy door anchored into the ground, thickening the glass on display cases or using a fog machine.

Sokka says it's critical to have integrated systems - so for example if an alarm goes off, you could shut down the facility, or lock down all high net worth paintings.

However, security measures are expensive. Mayor Caviezel, whose small French city hosts two museums and collections, says finding the money is "one of our main challenges".

"A small city can be entrusted with collections of national importance without having the financial resources of a major Parisian institution."

Bulut, who sits on the International Committee for Museum Security board, says it's not all about expensive gadgets. It could also be training guards to spot suspicious people who may be casing a museum and ask them if they need help, which may deter them from returning.

Museums are investing: Sokka says his company has seen an uptick in seismic offerings, that can detect vibration such as drilling in walls, in the past 18 months.

Museum heists are not increasing everywhere in Europe. In Sweden, major museum thefts began to decline around a decade ago and have not changed significantly in recent years, said Peg Magnusson, Sweden's representative for a Unesco convention to combat illicit trafficking of cultural property. However, other worrying cultural artefact targets have emerged.

The challenge for museums now is increasing security while also staying open to the public.

"A museum cannot be a fortress," Hollein says. "We want to be open institutions; at the same time, we are facing new challenges and attacks against museums that will require new standards."

Additional reporting by Madeleine Lake.

EntertainmentTab.title: Life after Eurovision Song Contest for Ramsgate's Look Mum No Computer
EntertainmentTab.text:
Representing the UK at the Eurovision Song Contest brought Sam Battle one point, but the musician has said the result is a "badge of honour".

Battle, better known by his stage name Look Mum No Computer, represented the UK at this year's Eurovision Song Contest with the electronic pop song Eins, Zwei, Drei.

Looking back on the competition, he said the experience passed in a blur. "It just happened so quick," he said. "I didn't even realise. I was just like, 'oh, I'm jumping on tables, don't fall off the table, Sam, sing'."

He was speaking ahead of his performance on Sunday at the Ramsgate Festival of Sound, external at the Granville Theatre where he plans to include Eins, Zwei, Drei in his set.

Reflecting on finishing at the bottom of the Eurovision scoreboard, Battle said many people had enjoyed the performance.

"I walk around and even a couple of days ago I was walking up to work and a couple of school kids were like, 'you were awesome'," he said.

"It's nice to know that I've made people smile."

Battle grew up in Yaxley, near Peterborough, but has made Ramsgate his home for the past eight years.

"It's great," he said. "I don't see myself going anywhere else."

He spends much of his time at This Museum Is (Not) Obsolete in the Kent town, which houses experimental and obsolete technology.

The museum's collection grew from years spent hunting for bargains at car boot sales and on internet sites.

A Furby organ and a 1960s telephone exchange are among his favourite items.

"You find bargains, you buy the bargains, you end up with loads of bargains and you're a hoarder," he said.

"And then you somehow find yourself in a situation where you can set up a museum and a hoarder is justified as a professional curator."

EntertainmentTab.title: Emily St John Mandel: ‘When half the electorate disagrees on basic reality, how do you come back from that?’
EntertainmentTab.text:
When Emily St John Mandel was a child she had a dream that would stay with her for decades. It was a nightmare in which “I was trying to find my dad in a crowd, and there were other people who looked like him but weren’t him”, she says. “It just kind of struck my imagination.”

Forty-ish years later, Mandel’s seventh novel, Exit Party, opens with a gathering in Los Angeles, 2031, where bizarre things happen. Doubles of some guests appear. Someone else disappears altogether. The novel then alternates between two potential future Americas, one riven by the chaos of civil war, the other a surveillance state.

Doppelgangers and alternative realities are having a cultural moment in our uncanny, deepfake times. Mandel says the biggest challenge western democracy faces is “the collapse of consensual reality. When you get to a situation where half the electorate disagrees on basic reality – for example, who won an election, or is Covid real? I don’t know how you come back from that.” On a more personal level, she has always been fascinated by what she calls “the counter-life – the one where you took a different job or married a different person. The way that, if we made a different decision, we would have become a somewhat different person.”

This interest comes, she thinks, from a feeling that “my life as a writer in New York City is a bit improbable”. Mandel was home-schooled on a tiny island in British Columbia, Canada, before training as a dancer. As she puts it, she was “essentially not educated until I was about 15 … I haven’t got a high school diploma.” She wrote while working office jobs until her third novel, Station Eleven, became a smash hit. The 2014 story of life after a global pandemic felt so prescient when readers rediscovered it during Covid that she developed a reputation for clairvoyance. It has sold 1.5m copies and been translated into 37 languages. Her novels since – The Glass Hotel and Sea of Tranquility – were global bestsellers too. It’s a staggering career, and, as she sees it: “There are a million ways this might not have happened.”

We meet on a sunny New York City day, in the lobby of a sleek Williamsburg hotel. Mandel, who lives in nearby Queens, wears a rose-printed shirt and comes across as warm yet precise. She’s off to have a haircut after we meet, even though her neat pixie cut scarcely looks trimmable.

One of the seeds of Exit Party was its protagonist Ari, who was the villain of Mandel’s second novel, 2010’s The Singer’s Gun. (Mandel is building a multiverse; characters reappear in Station Eleven, The Glass Hotel and Sea of Tranquility, though alas, she says, there is no Marvel movie coming.)

All these years later, “I just couldn’t stop thinking about her. I found myself thinking: what would that character be like at the other end of an 18-year prison sentence?” Ari is like a time traveller, she says; as we all are if we survive enough decades: “If you stick around long enough, you kind of become a migrant from a different timeline.”

Ari is a bit clairvoyant, something Mandel admits – with what I think may be a small wince – is based on her own experience. “I’ve had just a touch of that all my life. A tiny bit. It’s not nearly as useful as you might imagine. I absolutely cannot predict pandemics.” For example, when the March 2020 dates were announced for her Glass Hotel book tour, which was, of course, later cancelled, “I had a strange feeling: I would think about that tour, and it didn’t feel real. The best way I can describe the feeling is to say there was no life in it. When I thought about it, it was inert.” Or she might feel she needs scissors, and bring them to work – and realise she was right. “Dumb little examples like that,” she says, laughing: “Please don’t write that I’m psychic!”

Not psychic, then, but brilliant at imagining what might happen in our disaster-prone world. Even the writing process of this book was eerily predictive – though not in a straightforward way. When Mandel started writing, in spring 2022, she thought the civil war timeline was potentially “our near future. Not to be pessimistic but one reads the news.” Then she came up with an alternative, Universe B, to be “this kind of mirror image – totalitarianism instead of chaos”. By the time the book was nearing completion, with Trump’s bleak second presidency under way, “I felt like I was struggling to stay ahead of the news cycle in Universe B.” Citizens spy on one another and people are disappeared from the streets. “It’s been terrifying to see the speed with which the news cycle has caught up.”

Exit Party is Mandel’s third speculative novel. She is drawn to the form, she says, because she loves to “talk about the present by putting it in a sort of speculative cloak”. Sea of Tranquility, for example, “is absolutely a Covid-19 novel, but by setting it in the future on the moon, it was possible to write about it”. Realism would have been “frankly unbearable to write, let alone to read”. In Exit Party, too, she deftly creates emotional resonance through events that feel like a slanted take on our own times. The titular party, for example, takes place after a curfew is lifted, and has a vividly post-lockdown feel.

Her books come about, she says, through a process of “slow development”. She compares her first draft to a sculptor’s block of clay, “the raw material in which I’ll find the novel. There is no plan and no outline. I’ll start with a scene, build it up from there.” There are always moments when she thinks the novel is irretrievably broken, but she has never yet thrown a manuscript away. “I’ve always been able to change something that isn’t working into something that does work,” she says. Increasingly, she is bringing those skills to the screen, too, whether writing adaptations of her own work (she is working on the pilot for a TV adaptation of Exit Party), or staffing writers’ rooms – recently working on Netflix’s dramatisation of the video game Assassin’s Creed. She spends about one week in Los Angeles for every six in New York, often rising to write fiction in the morning, before an 11am writers’ room Zoom, “which is great in some ways and exhausting in others”.

Mandel recently had her own inflection point. Having divorced from her husband, a fellow writer, in 2022, she married photographer Laura Barisonzi in 2025. Their wedding was the stuff of book nerds’ dreams, held in Brooklyn’s Greenlight book store, which has been “hosting my launch events since before Station Eleven – and I didn’t sell many books back then!” They had an open book bar and her daughter, now 10, was a “ring bearer-slash-flower girl. It was just lovely.”

Exit Party, like much of her work, makes the case for relishing small moments of joy, frightening as the world is. That, she says, is “something I think about a lot. And maybe there’s a way of even appreciating good moments because they’re fleeting. That state of being temporary brings its own kind of sweetness.”

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘You start to worry you’ll never listen to anything else’: 25 years of Can’t Get You Out of My Head, the song that saw the future of pop
EntertainmentTab.text:
Around the release of Pet Shop Boys’ 1988 album Introspective, Neil Tennant coined the term “imperial phase” to describe an era when he felt the duo “understood the essence of pop music and so we felt we could do what we liked”. For his less flowery partner in pop excellence, Chris Lowe, this was typically followed “by disappearing up your backside!”.

In 2010, critic Tom Ewing fleshed out Tennant’s term by imposing three criteria: “command, permission, and self-definition”. Command related to an artist’s willingness and ability to push boundaries in a way that would reverberate through what followed. Permission, meanwhile, connected to the public and their goodwill towards an artist as they pushed things forward. Finally, self-definition, Ewing said, is the way the imperial phase defines the rest of the artist’s career. All future work will be compared with, or mentioned alongside, the output from the imperial phase.

By the time Kylie’s album Fever dropped, everything in its subsequent era represented her very own imperial phase. Everything she did in 2001 and 2002 seemed to click perfectly: every video, every choice of single, the tour, the press attention, the fashion, the cohesiveness of the vision, the way she reshaped pop and nudged it forward. And it was all led by the hypnotic weightlessness of the downright odd Can’t Get You Out of My Head.

The song was born one autumn weekend in 2000 in a garage studio in Surrey belonging to former Mud guitarist Rob Davis, who had been encouraged by manager and impresario Simon Fuller to write some songs with the excellent pop star turned songwriter Cathy Dennis.

On the Sunday, using Cubase on a Mac computer to create a drum loop before adding some guitar, the seed of Can’t Get You Out of My Head was planted. While Dennis came up with the title hook – the song, as she noted, doesn’t really conform to a typical verse-chorus structure, with each line almost acting as its own chorus melody – it was Davis who added the “‘la la la” section. The demo was finished in three hours, while Dennis’s vocals were laid down by 7pm that same day.

The demo was played to Fuller down the phone. He later played it for S Club 7, but they passed on it. The song was also presented to Sophie Ellis-Bextor, but again it was deemed unsuitable. It was Fuller’s idea to send it to Kylie. “And I was thinking: ‘But this song isn’t what Kylie does,’” remembered Dennis. “Obviously, now, none of us knows what Kylie’s going to come out with next, because she can’t be compartmentalised.” Kylie, meanwhile, “knew a few bars in that this was for me”, she wrote in 2002. “By the end of the track I wanted to know how quickly I could get into the studio.”

As promised, though much to Davis’s surprise given he’d convinced himself she wouldn’t turn up, Kylie arrived in Surrey to record Can’t Get You Out of My Head. In between some fancy salmon salad and other treats, the song was finished in a few hours. The mysterious pop alchemy of adding Kylie to a song took them all by surprise. “Even though Kylie wasn’t the first artist to be offered the song, I don’t believe it was meant to go to anyone other than Kylie,” said Dennis,“and I don’t believe anyone else would have done the incredible job she did with it, with the video, looking super-hot!”

Can’t Get You Out of My Head wasn’t just “good, for a pop song”, as joyless people were wont to say, keen to use the caveat in case their muso credentials be tarnished. As pop began to absorb the outre production styles of R&B experimentalists such as the Neptunes and Timbaland – Britney’s career-restructuring I’m a Slave 4 U, produced by the former, would arrive in the same month as Can’t Get You Out of My Head – audiences were becoming more attuned to pop that was looking to push the boundaries. This felt like dance-pop beamed in from the future, where the first time you hear it you’re like, “Huh?” then the second you’re like, “Wait!” and then the 35th time you start to worry you may never listen to anything else.

Its title becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. Can’t Get You Out of My Head’s sexy futurism would also dictate the visual feel of the era: sleek lines, icy-cool silhouettes and just a hint of something darker lurking underneath. For the album’s cover, shot by Vincent Peters, Kylie’s stylist and creative director William Baker was inspired by the French artist Jean-Paul Goude’s photos of Grace Jones, which highlighted both her sexuality and her power. Baker also wanted Kylie to be attached to the tools of her trade, so on both the album cover and artwork for Can’t Get You Out of My Head, a microphone’s black power cord winds its way round Kylie’s body.

Less overt than the buttock-hugging, Carry On vibes of Kylie’s previous album, Light Years, and its lead single, Spinning Around, the Fever look was leaning more into an artful sexiness. This was highlighted in Can’t Get You Out of My Head’s video, directed by Dawn Shadforth, in which the utopia promised by the millennium was laid out in front of us via forensically manicured cityscapes and futuristic fashion: we see her dance on what looks like a rooftop garden centre and in a clean white dome, and losing herself in a dress made of purple-silver Post-it notes.

It also gave Kylie yet another iconic fashion moment, one that would be replicated at gigs and fancy-dress parties for decades to come, in the shape of the white hooded dress, split to the navel.

While the dress grabbed the attention, it was the all-in-red dancers behind Kylie, sporting matching face-covering visors, who caused a problem for Top of the Pops producer Chris Cowey. As Can’t Get You Out of My Head started to dominate, the show’s lighting department began to complain that their red gels were going missing at the show’s on-set afterparty “because everyone was taking [them] and wrapping them around their heads and doing the dance”, Cowey says. “Just kind of drunkenly doing Kylie impersonations.”

By the early 2000s, after Oasis v Blur, the UK had become mildly obsessed with chart battles, ideally those featuring attractive women. On 17 September 2001, the same day as Can’t Get You Out of My Head, Victoria “Posh Spice” Beckham was set to release Not Such an Innocent Girl, the lead single from her self-titled debut solo album.

Posh had already been beaten, the previous year, by actually-quite-posh Sophie Ellis-Bextor, whose Rob Davis-assisted Groovejet (If This Ain’t Love) had left Beckham’s banger Out of Your Mind at No 2. This time, Victoria roared on to the battlefield with a ropey single and mildly scathing bons mots for her Australian rival. “When I first heard [Can’t Get You Out of My Head], if I’m being totally honest, I didn’t like it,” Posh mused. “And I’m being completely honest.”

For Posh, “an old-fashioned type songwriter”, Kylie’s single, while having “a very catchy melody”, didn’t resonate with her because she enjoys “a song that has a bit of emotion”. Posh was also retroactively blaming Kylie for criticisms of Out of Your Mind: “And I have to say that last year when I brought out a dance record, and I had effects on my voice, like she has on her voice, I am still getting a caning for it now.”

In the end, on the UK chart of 23 September, Can’t Get You Out of My Head crashed in at No 1, shifting an eye-watering 306,000 copies, holding off emerging talent Bob the Builder’s cover of Mambo No 5 in the process. It would stay at No 1 in the UK for a month, a feat matched in Australia. Posh’s Not Such an Innocent Girl would have to make do with a No 6 entry in the UK and sales of 35,000. The clash was such a hot topic that the BBC ran a news story with the headline: Kylie trounces Posh in chart battle. “Victoria is pleased to have a Top 10 hit,” a Posh spokeswoman was quoted as saying.

This particular pop star chart battle also served a specific escapist aim. Both singles were released shortly after 9/11, as the western world tried to recalibrate itself following a terrorist attack. The horrors seemed so overwhelming that any hint of normality was gripped tightly with both hands, and Can’t Get You Out of My Head’s futuristic escapism became a hypnotic balm.

For some journalists, the mere existence of Kylie was proof that Osama bin Laden and the Taliban could never win the “war on terror”. “Two people dominated the cultural landscape of this country in the last quarter of the year: Osama bin Laden and Kylie Minogue,” wrote Julie Burchill in the Guardian as 2001 came to an end. “I really do believe that Bin Laden and Kylie represent the polar opposites of human nature; the first all about cruelty without beauty, the second all about beauty without cruelty.”

Kylie was suddenly being held up as an emblem of western ideals – the literal face (and body) of the UK’s reaction to the global threat from a terrorist organisation. The Daily Mail printed a list of reasons to be cheerful, post-9/11, topped by Kylie. The picture they used alongside the piece was captioned “Fungirl Kylie, scourge of the Taliban”. Watching from the outside as this narrative unfolded, Kylie was “dumbfounded. I understand the way they’re seeing it as a positive thing, but no! Don’t write things like that!”

Actual human Kylie, not the projected superhero being pushed to the frontlines, was being interviewed live on local radio when the attacks took place. One of the DJs asked her on air, “So how does it feel to be a pop star in this situation?” “A two-second silence on live radio seems for ever,” Kylie remembered in the Face magazine. “I said: ‘I can’t believe you just asked me that.’ I think they swiftly cut to a record.”

Americans, at first, clung to a very different kind of superstar and song. Enrique Iglesias’s windswept ballad Hero, released on 3 September 2001, was one of the few songs played by New York City DJs after the attacks, but by the time Can’t Get You Out of My Head made its debut on the US charts in January 2002, a shift was happening. People needed something to dance to. “It was definitely at a time when people were gingerly going back [out],” remembers NYC music journalist Larry Flick. “I think [Can’t Get You Out of My Head] came at a time when we just needed Kylie, and an artist that wasn’t going to take it all too seriously. There were a few things, in New York, that got us through 9/11: there was the return of Friends, the return of David Letterman, and the Kylie record.”

Flick remembers the second time he heard it, in the Roxy, New York’s disco roller rink turned hip nightclub, which was famed as a venue that tested out new records. “I ran to the booth and I was like: ‘How about you playing Kylie?’ And the DJ goes: ‘Baby, this is the shit.’ He played it for about 20 minutes and the crowd lost their minds.”

Can’t Get You Out of My Head wasn’t just a hit; it was a smash. It didn’t just peak in all the usual places Kylie tended to, but also in places such as Belgium and Romania and Switzerland and Hungary. In the US, it quickly started to climb not just the Dance Club charts, where Kylie had been a regular, but also the main Billboard Hot 100, a chart she hadn’t been in since 1988.

“Can’t Get You Out of My Head was inescapable,” remembers US Kylie fan David Russell. “It started to get played on the radio, and then suddenly the video was on MTV. Kylie did Saturday Night Live with Ian McKellen hosting. I begged the publicist and she got me in. McKellen said: ‘You lucky, lucky people, it’s Kylie Minogue!’ He then sat on the side of the stage like a little kid watching her.”

Back in the UK, Kylie won twice at the 2002 Brit awards, scooping best international female and best international album for Fever. But it was her award-show performance that would gain instant notoriety, later becoming a mainstay of any homosexual’s post-night-out YouTube binge.

Performing a special mashup of Can’t Get You Out of My Head and New Order’s Blue Monday by then white-hot DJ and producer Erol Alkan, whose Trash club night was London’s hottest ticket, Kylie arrives on stage lying down on a giant CD – her name emblazoned on it in neon pink – seemingly holding on for dear life while wearing a Dolce & Gabbana minidress and knee-high silver boots. As the giant CD is ejected out of the player and lifts up so the crowd can see her for the first time, you’ll believe you can hear God. The performance was a perfect balancing act: audacious, spectacular, camp, sexy and silly in all the right ways.

“I feel like I’m on a wave and I actually know how to stand on the board at this point,” Kylie said as Can’t Get You Out of My Head and her imperial era kicked in. “I don’t know where it’s taking me, but everything feels really good.”

EntertainmentTab.title: Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom review – Aardman’s spooky-season caper sparkles with fun
EntertainmentTab.text:
Summer is over and Halloween is on the way … not for a fair bit, of course, but if all the UK’s Halloween merch and continuing pop culture content is up to the standard of this film, then no one is going to be complaining. This is the third in Aardman’s thoroughly enjoyable and cleverly written Shaun the Sheep stop-motion franchise of what are effectively silent movies, with a few intelligible words. It is the story of gutsy and heroic sheep involved in amazing adventures in the sleepy village of Mossy Bottom, starring characters who first appeared in the Wallace and Gromit short film A Close Shave.

This one is another excellent family film, crammed as ever with top visual gags, great throwaway references and, of course, a homemade Heath Robinson contraption, so often to be found in Aardman films. We get nods to The Archers, The Wombles and The Simpsons; there’s a wacky chase worthy of What’s Up, Doc?; a homage to the notorious waxing scene from Judd Apatow’s The 40-Year-Old Virgin; and even what appears to be a brief visual walk-on for George Bernard Shaw as Bigfoot. As ever with Shaun the Sheep and Aardman Animations generally, the standard of writing is extremely high and the script here, from Mark Burton and Giles Pilbrow, sparkles with good-natured fun. One high-street hairdressing salon in the wool-producing district where it’s set is called Barber Black Sheep – and if no real-life shop has stolen this joke yet, they ought to.

A klutzy, balding sheep farmer (voiced by John Sparkes), on whose premises Shaun and the gang are to be found, is poignantly in love with a visiting vet (voiced by Nina Sosanya); he longs to invite her to a local country music hoedown, but is shy and moreover ashamed of being follicularly challenged. As for the sheep themselves, they are secretly cultivating a pumpkin patch to harvest a bunch of scary jack-o-lanterns for their forthcoming Halloween frolics. The clumsy big-booted farmer ruins them all, and the resourceful sheep turn to the dark magic of technology and sinister GM techniques (as discovered in a children’s science book) to grow supersized new pumpkins from a rescued seed. But some of their occult new miracle growth-boost liquid finds its way into the farmer’s baldness-cure bottle.

The pitchfork-wielding villagers of Mossy Bottom are hilariously stunned at the terrifying appearance of a rampaging, hairy beast who has been spotted in the outlying fields and woodlands at the very moment that the farmer himself has mysteriously disappeared. Has the beast somehow kidnapped or eaten the farmer? It is a nightmarish mystery that will need every ounce of Shaun and his pals’ courage and ingenuity to sort out, not to mention that of the vet, who uses a hi-tech DNA machine to examine the genetic provenance of a piece of the beast’s fur she has managed to snip off.

It is a love story of sorts, perhaps a little like that of Beauty and the Beast, but about two people who for most the story’s running time don’t know that they are going to be in love. As for the sheep, their faces convey amazingly distinct expressions and moods with just a few deft movements. It’s sharp, smart, funny and precise; there is nothing woolly about it.

Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom is out on 17 September in Australia, and on 18 September in the UK and US.

GeneralTab.title: Andy Burnham among Great North Run 2026 finishers
GeneralTab.text:
The Great North Run (GNR) returned to Tyneside this weekend, with 63,000 runners taking part in the world's biggest half marathon - including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

England star and Newcastle captain Dan Burn rang the starter's bell, with famous faces including football personality Chris Kamara and fitness coach Joe Wicks taking on the challenge.

The 13.1-mile (21km) event saw runners and wheelchair users race from Newcastle through Gateshead and South Tyneside, before finishing in South Shields.

Britons David Weir and Melanie Woods won the men's and women's elite wheelchair races respectively. Brigid Kosgei won the elite women's contest and Zouhair Talbi won the men's race.

The half marathon is in its 45th year and raises about £25m for charity each time.

The prime minister said he was "very happy" with his finish time of under two hours - 01.57 - and was raising money for North East charity Changing Lives, which he visited last month to launch a national drive to end rough sleeping.

"You see the causes people are running for, all pulling together for the bigger cause," Burnham said. "It's just a day that reminds you how good this country is when it's together like this.

"This part of the world, it doesn't half shine on a day like this. The warmth of the people comes out - the people in the race with you, the people on the sidelines."

As always, runners donned a variety of costumes in the bid to raise funds for good causes. Among them were nuns, horses and a pair of ovaries.

The 2026 medal was designed by local artist Alex Mulholland - known as Mul - and features the Tyne Bridge.

"The design celebrates the stories behind each runner, and the incredible causes that inspire so many people to take on the event," he said.

GeneralTab.title: 'Slim chance' government will hit 1.5m new homes target, Rayner tells BBC
GeneralTab.text:
There is only a "slim chance" the government will meet its target of building 1.5 million homes in England by the next election, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has told the BBC.

"Headwinds" including the Iran war and rising construction costs are making it harder to meet the key Labour manifesto pledge, Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.

"But I'm definitely not giving it up," she said, and stressed that the government was "making a difference" through investing billions in social and affordable homes.

Data up to June this year suggested the government was behind on the rate of construction needed to meet the goal, which housebuilders have previously warned was too optimistic.

Labour promised to hit the target through building both private and social housing by the end of the current parliament, meaning summer 2029 at the latest.

This implied an average of 300,000 new properties would be needed each year - a rate of construction not seen in decades.

Rayner told the BBC on Sunday: "It's a slim chance, but I'm definitely not giving it up."

She said it was important to keep the goal - which she said had always been a "stretch target" - in place, but that she was "being honest with the public" that it would be difficult to achieve.

"The prime minister wants us to make sure we're building council houses. He's made that absolutely, fundamentally clear," she said.

"We're seeing home starts up by 15% last year, so we are making a difference."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period" - although he has not provided details on exactly what this will entail.

BBC Verify analysis showed a decline in the number of new houses being built during Labour's first year in power - continuing a fall that began under the Conservatives.

Rayner's predecessor in the role, Steve Reed, last year admitted a sharp surge in construction would be needed to reach the goal - but said he expected it would just about be met once the impact of planning reforms took hold.

Analysts have said reforms introduced by Sir Keir Starmer's government should help increase construction in the long term, including changing the rules on green belt development to increase the area in which homes can be built.

But some argue that construction is being held back by factors including high house prices relative to average incomes, higher costs due to global conflict and labour shortages since Brexit.

BBC Verify has been tracking performance against the target using government data on Energy Performance Certificates (EPC). Each newly created dwelling must have an EPC by law, making it the most timely indicator of new homes being built.

Data for the 12 months to June 2026 suggested about 203,000 new homes were delivered in England that year, far short of the 300,000 needed to meet the target.

GeneralTab.title: Trump: US president doubles down on united Ireland comments on day two of visit
GeneralTab.text:
President Donald Trump has doubled down on his support for a united Ireland.

He's on day two of a visit, which he is spending at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg, County Clare, for the Irish Open.

On Saturday, Trump told reporters he would love to see a united Ireland while at a meeting with the Taoiseach (Irish PM) Micheál Martin in Dublin.

Speaking on Sunday at his Doonbeg golf resort, he said it would be natural to put Ireland and Northern Ireland "together".

He spoke to reporters after watching the tournament leader Irish golfer Shane Lowry tee off.

He described what he said about a united Ireland as "a fairly routine comment".

"I've always loved the people of Ireland. It just seems to me you have Northern Ireland and Ireland," he said

"It seems that one of the naturals of all time is to put them together.

"That's only my opinion, and by the way many people agree."

The president sidestepped a question about Scottish independence.

"I won't talk about Scotland yet I will save that," he said.

The taoiseach said the president's remarks did not come as a "surprise" to him.

Speaking on Sunday at The Open, Martin referred to Trump asking about a "merger" of Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland at an event in Washington during the Saint Patrick's Day celebrations, which some believed to be a comment on unity.

"He would make the point this is his view. He believes unity is the logical way for the island to be configured and organised," Martin said.

A major security operation is continuing for Trump's visit to Ireland.

He will leave from Shannon Airport on Sunday evening.

More than 10,000 people marched through Dublin on Saturday to show their opposition to the US president.

Others protesting against the visit have been arriving in buses to Doonbeg on Sunday, with about 100 protesters present.

A small crowd were moved from the president's hotel by Gardai (Irish police), Irish broadcaster RTÉ is reporting.

On Saturday evening, three women were arrested for trespassing on the golf links at Doonbeg and appeared at a special sitting of Ennis District Court.

Rev Steven Foster, a Methodist minister from Galway, attended the anti-Trump protest in Doonbeg.

"I'm here because Trump is the exact opposite of everything I stand for as a follower of Jesus," he told BBC News NI.

Seoirse Comerford owns the Comerford bar in Doonbeg. He described the tournament as "unbelievable".

"If you look at the red double decker buses going up and down the street full of people, we never thought we would have seen the like of that."

He said the golf course is a big employer and is keeping Doonbeg "alive".

"Most rural villages in west Clare are all dying a death, young people going away to college, they don't come back.

"Like there's over 300 people employed up there at the golf course , it's a big boost to the local economy. You've got big companies in Dublin, like Intel, the golf course is our Intel down here.

"I probably wouldn't have taken over the bar business other than the golf course being up there.

"We would have had 1,000 plus through the pub on Saturday night and the same Friday night, so there's a lot of people around the village, which is great to see."

GeneralTab.title: Reform's £72m donations 'entirely in line with law', Jenrick says
GeneralTab.text:
Reform UK believes the £72m in donations it has received from two cryptocurrency billionaires were "entirely in line with the law", the party's economic spokesman has said.

Robert Jenrick told the BBC he did not expect that the party will have to return any of the money from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British and have spent time living overseas.

The government is seeking to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British expats, including a £100,000 cap backdated to 25 March.

"These two donations are entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, the law as it's going to be in the future," Jenrick said.

As well as limiting how much British citizens can donate to political parties from overseas, the government has proposed a minimum residency period in which the £100,000 cap would still apply for those who move back to the UK.

This would be in place for the remainder of the calendar year and the following calendar year after the person returns.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that the rule changes would apply retrospectively and anyone not complying with them would have "to return that money".

Rayner added she was not commenting specifically on Delo and Harborne as she does not "understand" their "circumstances".

Answering questions about the donations following Rayner's remarks, Jenrick said: "It might be that Angela Rayner or the government keep trying to change the law to make it even harder for people to donate to Reform, nothing would surprise me.

"But, as it stands, we believe these are entirely in line with the law."

BBC News has been told that both Delo and Harborne have returned to the UK. Delo is understood to have been back in the country since last year.

Jenrick said Delo had returned to the UK "in part so that he can comply with the changes to the law".

In a statement after the programme, a Reform UK spokesman said: "We are 100% confident both [donations] are legal and won't ever have to handed back."

One person familiar with the government's proposed changes said the issue of whether Delo and Harborne are affected would likely come down to how ministers choose to define UK residency.

They said one way would be to adopt the same definition used in tax laws, but stressed how complex the rules around residency are.

The government's proposed changes were added to the Representation of the People Bill after they were approved by MPs this month. The bill still needs to be scrutinised in the House of Lords.

Rayner said the proposals were "directly as a result" of a review by former top civil servant Philip Rycroft, external, published on 25 March.

Rayner said: "We said that because of the intention of the legislation and the recommendations, which we accepted, was known in the public domain that it would be retrospective to that date.

"That legislation is going through Parliament at the moment and we've also written to the Electoral Commission, which is an independent body, to see what further measures we need to take to protect our democracy."

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.

The government has previously said it was "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors", and has established a new taskforce to do this.

It did not support calls from some MPs for a cap but Rayner left the door open to the possibility of further restrictions.

"It's not as simple as we're saying we won't put a cap [on donations], it's a question of making sure that the task and finish group look at how we implement this."

Rayner said the aim would be to "protect our democracy in the spirit of individuals not being able to overpower and buy their way into democracy at the expense of those people that are at the ballot box".

Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said it was important to ensure "we do not end up with a sort of Americanisation of politics where money just sort of runs free".

He said people should be able to support the democratic movements they wished but added that "what we've got to be careful about is where different industries, where different financial sources raise questions".

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart said there should be emergency legislation to cap campaign donations and spending.

She said: "No politician should be able to buy the keys to Number 10."

A Green Party spokesperson said there needed to be "more robust laws" around political donations, adding: "The Labour Party urgently needs to find its spine and support a tight cap on donations from individuals."

Jenrick said Delo and Harborne - who each gave £36m to the party in two days and now share the record for the largest ever donation given to a UK political party - were "not buying anything, they simply support our agenda".

Both men had already donated millions of pounds to Reform ahead of the announcement of their latest contributions.

The Times reported in June that Harborne, who has been based in Thailand, had registered to vote in the UK, while Delo had told the Telegraph in April that he was moving back from Hong Kong.

Harborne wrote in the Telegraph on Saturday that Reform was a "start-up party" that lacked "the benefit of hundreds of years of patronage". Delo had written in the newspaper the day prior that he wanted to enable Reform to put up a "fair fight at the next election.

The £72m from the two is more than the total received by all UK political parties last year.

Delo was pardoned by US President Donald Trump last year over a breach of anti-money laundering laws at his crypto trading platform, BitMex, to which he had pleaded guilty in 2022.

Reform's fundraising has come under scrutiny in recent months. This includes police announcing an investigation over allegations the party broke foreign funding laws in a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week.

The party's leader Nigel Farage is also under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner over whether he should have declared a £5m gift he received from Harborne ahead of the 2024 election.

Both Reform and Farage have denied any wrongdoing in both instances.

GeneralTab.title: US prices remain high as fuel costs squeeze household budgets
GeneralTab.text:
Prices in the US rose by 3.4% in the year to August, with the cost of living pushed up by higher gasoline prices, official figures show.

The overall inflation rate was unchanged from July, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).

It comes ahead of the Federal Reserve making its latest interest rate decision next week, with growing expectations they will be increased in a bid to slow the rate at which prices are rising.

US household budgets have come under mounting pressure, especially at the fuel pumps, with a gallon of diesel hitting a new all-time high of more than $6 on average on Friday.

The spike in fuel prices has been driven by higher global oil prices, caused by supply disruptions as a result of the US-Iran war. The price of benchmark Brent crude oil is hovering above $100 a barrel following recent escalations in the conflict.

As well as directly driving up costs at the pumps, higher oil prices can also make transporting goods more expensive. Such costs can be passed down to consumers through steeper prices for food and other staples, pushing up the overall cost of living.

The BLS said gasoline prices rose 3.9% last month alone, accounting for more than a third of inflation overall. Wages are also failing to keep up with the rising cost of living, with separate figures showing real average hourly earnings fell by 0.3% over the past year.

There are increasing expectations that interest rates will be hiked given the current inflation picture, strong jobs market and President Donald Trump saying he does not think oil prices will come down until the war with Iran ends, which he expects to happen after November's elections.

Fed chair Kevin Warsh has been tight-lipped on any future decisions, but his comments that the central bank's focus should be on slowing price rises has further fuelled expectations of a rise.

According to data from CME Group, 85% of traders are now betting on rates being raised by a quarter percentage point next week.

articles.title: Andy Burnham among Great North Run 2026 finishers
articles.text:
The Great North Run (GNR) returned to Tyneside this weekend, with 63,000 runners taking part in the world's biggest half marathon - including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

England star and Newcastle captain Dan Burn rang the starter's bell, with famous faces including football personality Chris Kamara and fitness coach Joe Wicks taking on the challenge.

The 13.1-mile (21km) event saw runners and wheelchair users race from Newcastle through Gateshead and South Tyneside, before finishing in South Shields.

Britons David Weir and Melanie Woods won the men's and women's elite wheelchair races respectively. Brigid Kosgei won the elite women's contest and Zouhair Talbi won the men's race.

The half marathon is in its 45th year and raises about £25m for charity each time.

The prime minister said he was "very happy" with his finish time of under two hours - 01.57 - and was raising money for North East charity Changing Lives, which he visited last month to launch a national drive to end rough sleeping.

"You see the causes people are running for, all pulling together for the bigger cause," Burnham said. "It's just a day that reminds you how good this country is when it's together like this.

"This part of the world, it doesn't half shine on a day like this. The warmth of the people comes out - the people in the race with you, the people on the sidelines."

As always, runners donned a variety of costumes in the bid to raise funds for good causes. Among them were nuns, horses and a pair of ovaries.

The 2026 medal was designed by local artist Alex Mulholland - known as Mul - and features the Tyne Bridge.

"The design celebrates the stories behind each runner, and the incredible causes that inspire so many people to take on the event," he said.

articles.title: 'Slim chance' government will hit 1.5m new homes target, Rayner tells BBC
articles.text:
There is only a "slim chance" the government will meet its target of building 1.5 million homes in England by the next election, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has told the BBC.

"Headwinds" including the Iran war and rising construction costs are making it harder to meet the key Labour manifesto pledge, Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.

"But I'm definitely not giving it up," she said, and stressed that the government was "making a difference" through investing billions in social and affordable homes.

Data up to June this year suggested the government was behind on the rate of construction needed to meet the goal, which housebuilders have previously warned was too optimistic.

Labour promised to hit the target through building both private and social housing by the end of the current parliament, meaning summer 2029 at the latest.

This implied an average of 300,000 new properties would be needed each year - a rate of construction not seen in decades.

Rayner told the BBC on Sunday: "It's a slim chance, but I'm definitely not giving it up."

She said it was important to keep the goal - which she said had always been a "stretch target" - in place, but that she was "being honest with the public" that it would be difficult to achieve.

"The prime minister wants us to make sure we're building council houses. He's made that absolutely, fundamentally clear," she said.

"We're seeing home starts up by 15% last year, so we are making a difference."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period" - although he has not provided details on exactly what this will entail.

BBC Verify analysis showed a decline in the number of new houses being built during Labour's first year in power - continuing a fall that began under the Conservatives.

Rayner's predecessor in the role, Steve Reed, last year admitted a sharp surge in construction would be needed to reach the goal - but said he expected it would just about be met once the impact of planning reforms took hold.

Analysts have said reforms introduced by Sir Keir Starmer's government should help increase construction in the long term, including changing the rules on green belt development to increase the area in which homes can be built.

But some argue that construction is being held back by factors including high house prices relative to average incomes, higher costs due to global conflict and labour shortages since Brexit.

BBC Verify has been tracking performance against the target using government data on Energy Performance Certificates (EPC). Each newly created dwelling must have an EPC by law, making it the most timely indicator of new homes being built.

Data for the 12 months to June 2026 suggested about 203,000 new homes were delivered in England that year, far short of the 300,000 needed to meet the target.

articles.title: Trump: US president doubles down on united Ireland comments on day two of visit
articles.text:
President Donald Trump has doubled down on his support for a united Ireland.

He's on day two of a visit, which he is spending at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg, County Clare, for the Irish Open.

On Saturday, Trump told reporters he would love to see a united Ireland while at a meeting with the Taoiseach (Irish PM) Micheál Martin in Dublin.

Speaking on Sunday at his Doonbeg golf resort, he said it would be natural to put Ireland and Northern Ireland "together".

He spoke to reporters after watching the tournament leader Irish golfer Shane Lowry tee off.

He described what he said about a united Ireland as "a fairly routine comment".

"I've always loved the people of Ireland. It just seems to me you have Northern Ireland and Ireland," he said

"It seems that one of the naturals of all time is to put them together.

"That's only my opinion, and by the way many people agree."

The president sidestepped a question about Scottish independence.

"I won't talk about Scotland yet I will save that," he said.

The taoiseach said the president's remarks did not come as a "surprise" to him.

Speaking on Sunday at The Open, Martin referred to Trump asking about a "merger" of Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland at an event in Washington during the Saint Patrick's Day celebrations, which some believed to be a comment on unity.

"He would make the point this is his view. He believes unity is the logical way for the island to be configured and organised," Martin said.

A major security operation is continuing for Trump's visit to Ireland.

He will leave from Shannon Airport on Sunday evening.

More than 10,000 people marched through Dublin on Saturday to show their opposition to the US president.

Others protesting against the visit have been arriving in buses to Doonbeg on Sunday, with about 100 protesters present.

A small crowd were moved from the president's hotel by Gardai (Irish police), Irish broadcaster RTÉ is reporting.

On Saturday evening, three women were arrested for trespassing on the golf links at Doonbeg and appeared at a special sitting of Ennis District Court.

Rev Steven Foster, a Methodist minister from Galway, attended the anti-Trump protest in Doonbeg.

"I'm here because Trump is the exact opposite of everything I stand for as a follower of Jesus," he told BBC News NI.

Seoirse Comerford owns the Comerford bar in Doonbeg. He described the tournament as "unbelievable".

"If you look at the red double decker buses going up and down the street full of people, we never thought we would have seen the like of that."

He said the golf course is a big employer and is keeping Doonbeg "alive".

"Most rural villages in west Clare are all dying a death, young people going away to college, they don't come back.

"Like there's over 300 people employed up there at the golf course , it's a big boost to the local economy. You've got big companies in Dublin, like Intel, the golf course is our Intel down here.

"I probably wouldn't have taken over the bar business other than the golf course being up there.

"We would have had 1,000 plus through the pub on Saturday night and the same Friday night, so there's a lot of people around the village, which is great to see."

articles.title: US embassy child abuse images suspect flown from UK before police interview
articles.text:
A US embassy staffer accused of possessing indecent images of children, was detained at his south London flat and flown out of the UK in August, without being first questioned by British police.

The US Embassy confirmed to the BBC that authorities are investigating the allegations and they have reassigned the staff member to the US while inquiries continue.

"The United States government expects all personnel to adhere to the highest standards of conduct, and we take these allegations seriously," embassy officials said in a statement.

They added that they "quickly informed UK law enforcement and took swift action."

It is understood the individual worked at the US embassy in Vauxhall, south west London, and though not a diplomat, he enjoyed the umbrella of diplomatic protection.

He was flown back to the United States on a commercial flight, but their investigations are ongoing in conjunction with UK authorities.

It is also understood Home Office ministers and the Metropolitan Police are in close contact with the US embassy on this matter as investigations continue.

A UK government spokesperson said: "We expect all foreign diplomats in the UK to abide by our laws, in the same way we expect all UK diplomats to do so when posted overseas."

articles.title: Some dentists say more young people are grinding their teeth - are you one of them?
articles.text:
Ella can't remember when she first started grinding her teeth at night, but she can vividly recall the excruciating jaw ache, the headaches, and being told her molars were disappearing.

"I was in so much pain," Ella says. "My face was changing shape and my teeth were at risk of breaking - I knew I had to do something about it."

The 31-year-old has bruxism, a condition which can cause regular and often intense teeth grinding, but says the treatment she's recently had has "without a doubt" changed her life.

Bruxism affects millions like Ella across the UK, external. Some studies suggest nearly one in four people experience the condition, although many may be unaware until symptoms appear.

According to the British Dental Association there is some anecdotal evidence that bruxism is becoming more common, but no specific figures. However, some dentists have told the BBC they are worried about the increasing number of young people they're seeing with dental problems caused by incessant gnashing.

"It is definitely on the rise," Dr Aditi Desai, president of the British Society of Dental Sleep Medicine (BSDSM), says. "And it's no surprise given that life itself nowadays can be so stressful."

Studies, external suggest many of us Bruxers do it because of stress - but why do our jaws carry the burden of our everyday lives? What can we do about it? And can it actually be a good thing in some cases?

Bruxism is an umbrella term which groups together four different jaw movements - clenching, grinding, bracing and thrusting.

Some people grind at night, others through the day. Some barely notice they're doing it, while others can gnash through mouthguards and wake even the deepest sleeping bed partners.

So how can you tell if you do it? Here are the signs to look out for:

Worn, chipped or flattened teeth

Headaches or facial pain in the morning

Disrupted sleep and daytime tiredness

Increased tooth sensitivity

Earache or pain near the temples without infection

Teeth grinding is also mentioned more frequently in therapy according to the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy, which says people nowadays are more aware of how their mental health impacts their body.

Psychotherapist Rahi Popat says more of his clients - particularly younger ones - say they or someone else have noticed they've been grinding their teeth, "and they can often link that to a really stressful time in their lives and realise that's when their teeth grinding either increased or even started".

Trauma and stress can put you in "fight or flight" mode, where your heart rate increases, you release adrenaline, and your muscles tense, preparing the body for an external threat, he says. And because the jaw and the nervous system are so closely linked through the major cranial nerves, our muscles are triggered and we clench and grind our teeth.

"If we do it overnight, it's a way of our bodies releasing some of the stress and tension we might have felt through the day," Popat explains.

For Ella, nocturnal teeth grinding in her sleep became a way to release tension that had built up while she was awake.

"I know it's to do with my stress levels," Ella says. "I have high functioning anxiety - you wouldn't think it if you met me.

"I'm busy, and I go out a lot to mask it."

In her 20s, she says she just "put up" with the pain. But a few years later, when her dentist told her that her teeth were at risk, Ella decided to get treatment.

Even though it's not routinely offered on the NHS, Ella decided to pay her dentist to inject Botox into her masseter muscles - the ones that control her jaw. The procedure relaxed them and reduced the tension in her face, and should last 3 to 4 months.

"Over the past few months I've been able to sleep properly," she says. "I've got so much more energy in the mornings, the pain has reduced and my face is not as square."

Dr Simon Cove, a dentist who treats both private and NHS patients, says the physical impact of grinding on our teeth can be huge.

He uses a 3D scanner to assess his patients' teeth, and can see the wear over time.

"Often people are not even aware they are doing it, but then we get to see the damage," he says. "If the teeth have been worn down to such an extent, treatment can be extremely complex and can cost thousands of pounds."

But he says such cases are relatively uncommon and can take years to develop.

Dentist Riaz Yar, a specialist in prosthodontics, treats patients struggling with the effects of severe bruxism - worn, cracked and fractured teeth, and dental work that keeps failing. Many also arrive with chronic jaw or facial pain and report poor sleep, all of which need assessing in their own right, he says, rather than simply being blamed on the grinding.

In the past, Yar says, teeth grinding was considered simply a mechanical problem of the jaw, but now there is strong evidence that it is much more complex. It's a "biopsychosocial issue", he says, driven by the brain and nervous system and shaped by the whole person.

"We take into account their sleep patterns, their diet, their weight, the amount they exercise, what medication they might be taking and we assess for signs of sleep disorders," he says. "Many factors can contribute to a patient grinding their teeth, so addressing the condition requires a multidisciplinary approach."

How best to tackle it? These things might help:

Mouthguard to wear at night to protect your teeth

If linked to sleep apnoea, devices such as a CPAP machine or a mandibular advancement device (MAD) to help keep the airway open

Talking therapies such as CBT

Lifestyle changes to help reduce stress and improve sleep such as exercise, cutting down on alcohol, stopping smoking and eating healthier

For severe cases Botox is an option, but it's rarely available on the NHS

Along with muscle-relaxing injections, Ella says she is also meditating to try to reduce her anxiety and free herself from the tension she regularly carries.

"Having treatment has transformed my life," Ella says, "now I want to try and figure out the root cause."

articles.title: Will the Thirlwall report change the debate about Lucy Letby?
articles.text:
Mention Lucy Letby and you're likely to get a strong reaction.

The nurse was sentenced to spend the rest of her life in prison for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more.

But though two juries have convicted her, and she has twice been denied permission to appeal, it seems everyone has an opinion on whether she really did it.

There's loud scepticism about her convictions from some, and vocal certainty about her guilt from others. She has become the centre of an information war.

The name Lady Justice Thirlwall, however, attracts less recognition.

The quick take is this. The report won't change the narrative about Letby's guilt or innocence because it didn't examine that subject at all. That wasn't its remit.

Lady Justice Thirlwall said she had "approached the inquiry on the basis that Lucy Letby is guilty of the crimes of which she has been convicted".

She emphasised that it was not her role "to set about reviewing the convictions", telling the inquiry: "The Court of Appeal has done that, with a very clear result."

But there is also a longer, more complex answer.

Whatever the report's conclusions, Letby's convictions will stand. However, the inquiry hasn't operated in a vacuum. There are other parts of the legal system which will have an eye on its findings.

And the chairwoman of the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) - the only organisation with the power to send Letby's case back to the Court of Appeal - has told the BBC the CCRC will be paying close attention to Thirlwall.

Dame Vera Baird said: "We will be looking at the report with interest to assess whether it has any bearing on our review of the case."

The CCRC has given no indication of when it will make its decision.

But while questions over Letby's convictions weren't within the scope of the Thirlwall Inquiry, it didn't stop the subject making itself felt within the hearing room.

Just as the inquiry was wrapping up, the hospital's former executives applied for it to be delayed until the CCRC has made its decision.

Letters pushing for a delay were also written to the inquiry by Letby's lawyers and Sir David Davis, an MP who has campaigned on her behalf.

Sir David argued that an inquiry "predicated on the presumption that Lucy Letby's conviction is safe, when there is now a wealth of authoritative voices questioning that conviction, will only undermine the conclusions arrived at by your inquiry and potentially lead to more babies dying unnecessarily".

Lady Justice Thirlwall refused the requests to pause the inquiry. She said that she was not scrutinising Letby's actions, but those of the officials and managers who were responsible for responding to the crisis.

The most stark question it may answer is whether any babies might have lived, or avoided injury, if action had been taken earlier.

The inquiry released thousands of documents which shed new light on what was going on inside the hospital. When the hearings finished, we put together this timeline which illustrates how events unfolded.

Should alarm bells have started ringing as early as June 2015 when three babies died in quick succession – the same number of deaths within two weeks that the unit would normally expect in a year? What about in August 2015, when a baby was poisoned with insulin?

The results of his blood test didn't raise an alert. At the inquiry, hospital consultants accepted this had been a "collective failure".

Lawyers for the baby's family said the test results "provided the clearest opportunity to detect and stop Letby" and were "a bright line within the chronology after which no babies should have been harmed".

By early 2016, senior managers including medical director Ian Harvey and director of nursing Alison Kelly knew there was an unusually high death rate on the neonatal unit and that there were escalating concerns about a nurse. But it didn't lead to safeguarding action.

It was only after two triplet brothers died in June 2016 that Letby was taken off nursing duty.

Thirlwall will also make recommendations for change. These could include new controls on the storage of insulin; compulsory procedures to be followed when deliberate harm is suspected; detail on the regulation of NHS managers and executives; and greater use of CCTV within neonatal units.

She will also expose the number of recommendations made by public inquiries into more than 30 previous NHS scandals, which have not been followed.

Analysis by the inquiry's legal team showed that, of more than 1,400 recommendations made by previous healthcare-related inquiries, the majority have not been clearly implemented.

Solicitor Richard Scorer refers to the failure to implement recommendations from public inquiries as "the British disease".

"It is a betrayal not just of the people who have suffered in these cases, families like those I represent, it's actually betrayal of the public," he said.

Journalist David James Smith, who is a former CCRC Commissioner, says the commission will be paying attention to the Thirlwall report "for any evidence that supports or undermines the convictions and supports or undermines the submissions it has received on Letby's behalf".

Cheshire Police will also have a close eye on the Thirlwall report. A criminal investigation into three hospital executives is still underway. They were previously arrested on suspicion of gross negligence manslaughter, and one of them has since been rearrested on suspicion of perverting the course of justice.

It's likely that detectives will look closely at the inquiry's findings about those managers, which could be factored into their investigation.

And then there is the public debate.

As the legal wheels have been turning in the background, those campaigning to free Letby have redoubled their efforts, with protests and websites dedicated to her cause. But there are also strong feelings from those who believe she belongs in jail. Both sides have found energy online, within highly active forums on Facebook, Reddit, Tattle Life, and elsewhere.

How will Lady Justice Thirlwall's report go down with those communities?

David Wilson, emeritus professor of criminology at Birmingham City University, believes it's unlikely that the report will reverse hard-baked opinions.

"The 'noisier' Letby commentators are almost universally on the side that she is innocent," he says. "I have no doubt there will be aspects of the governance of the hospital where she killed within the report that will be harnessed to support that view."

Prof Wilson believes it will become "another component of the information war that's constantly being waged about her guilt or innocence" and he feels much of the conversation about Letby "seems to generate more heat than light".

One thing is certain. No matter what their point of view, everyone with a strong opinion about Letby will pay close attention to the report. Even those who wanted it to be delayed, or who didn't support it in the first place, will scour its findings.

But it's much less likely to take the heat out of the public debate or draw a line under the case. Those who say they're already sure about Lucy Letby may scrutinise the report, but take from it whatever supports those ready-formed views.

articles.title: Meena and Minal: Best friends for decades - until a DNA test revealed they were sisters
articles.text:
Theirs is a story straight out of a Bollywood film.

Two Indian-born women in their 40s, adopted as babies by different families and raised near each other in the Netherlands, have now discovered they are biological sisters.

Meena Geltink and Minal Tijssen, born in the early 1980s, were adopted from two different orphanages in the western Indian city of Mumbai within months of their birth.

When they first met in their early teens at an event hosted by the adoption agency their parents had used, they were struck by the uncanny similarities in their appearance and mannerisms.

Meena, now 43, remembers the day clearly.

"All the adopted children were brought together to hang out and bond and have dinner."

Both Meena and Minal were with friends who noticed how similar they looked.

"They said, 'Look at yourselves in the mirror'.

"And I was like, 'Oh my God, she has my nose! We have the same laugh'.

"At dinner, I kept looking at her the whole time," Meena told the BBC from her home in the Netherlands.

The following day, the girls exchanged telephone numbers and addresses and promised to keep in touch.

Even though there was no indication they were related by blood, their connection was instant, and for years they wrote each other letters, often addressing each other as "Sis" because "we felt that way".

They wrote about school, friends, boys, going out and dancing. They told each other about the sports they played and discussed music, discovering they both loved Backstreet Boys.

Then 15 years ago, they lost contact. Minal had moved to France. And Meena had recently had her first child and got busy.

In 2017, Meena attended another meeting of adoptees from India where she heard about DNA testing and decided to take a test herself. But she never found any matches and earlier this year, deleted the app because her phone storage was full. Then on 20 May, Meena received a message from Minal on Facebook.

"'Remember me?' she asked.

Minal had taken a DNA test in April while visiting her parents in the Netherlands and attached a screengrab of her test result.

"I reinstalled the app. I was so nervous I entered wrong passwords 10 times before I was able to log in," Meena says.

The result couldn't have been clearer - the two women were "a 100% match".

"I had a 'full sister' which means we shared the same biological mother and father," Meena explains. "It was like I had an adrenalin shot. I cried. Minal was my missing puzzle piece I had waited so long for. We had called each other sister.

"This DNA match was the confirmation that all our intuition was right."

On a fine sunny day in August the old friends met for the first time since discovering they were sisters.

"It was amazing. It felt like homecoming," Meena, now a mother to three children, says. "For years, Minal and I had felt a big hole in our hearts. We feel like we've been completed. Everything now feels like it's supposed to be."

Reporting on their "emotional reunion", Reuters said "tears, hugs ​and laughter punctuated their ​meeting... followed by their first selfie together".

Minal, 44, who lives in France with her partner and two sons, told the agency that when her ⁠DNA results came in April, she had initially not realised her match was the same teenage girl who had clung to her when ​they first met 30 years ago.

It only sank in when she looked at her photos on social media. "'Meena: Sister.' I couldn't believe it. We were friends before we were sisters.

"We were sisters the whole time," she said, "but we didn't know."

Since May, Meena and Minal have been speaking every other day. They've met each other's spouses, children, brothers and parents.

"Everyone notices how we finish each other's sentences, how we move our heads or walk similar," Meena says.

The fact they are siblings is still sinking in, she says.

"Sometimes we talk for two hours and lose track of time, suddenly remembering that we have to do groceries or pick up children from school."

One thing she and her sister would "love to do", Meena says, is return to the place where it all began.

"We'd love to go to India together sometime, to walk through the streets of Mumbai together.

"There were times when we both felt very lonely, like when I lost my dad or went through a heartbreak," she says.

"I regret we couldn't be with each other - we could have shared happiness, helped each other in tough times."
