articles.title: Tensions simmer on US-Canada border for two towns relying on each other
articles.text:
Like many Canadians, Tom Reid isn’t crossing the US-Canada border as often these days. But he needed a haircut.

The woman who cuts his hair lives in International Falls, Minnesota – her “sister is married to my wife’s cousin”, he explained – and so Reid, whose duty free shop in Fort Frances, Ontario, has to travel to her.

That’s how it goes for the residents of the two towns, divided by the Rainy River and an international border. They’re longtime friends and, in many cases, family. People cross the border frequently to shop, dine, go bowling, take their kids to sports and visit each other.

But Trump’s trade war against the US’s northern neighbor, and his derogatory comments about their country, has Canadians – known for their politeness – angry. Furious, actually. They’re shopping less at US businesses, and, in an unusual show of patriotism, encouraging consumers to “buy Canadian instead”.

Reid is buying Canadian more and more, he said at the register in his shop, with the Canadian flag on the wall behind him. “I don’t have that much choice, eh?” he said.

American business owners have seen declines in Canadian sales, while grappling with the uncertainty and costs associated with tariffs on their products. With tourist season winding down, and the leaves starting to change into yellows and oranges, the two towns are quieter.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs went into force this week, though no one who lived in the towns had seen that directly reflected in prices yet. It was the latest heated battle between the two countries in the last nearly two years.

The mayors of the two towns call each other friends, and signed a joint declaration in 2025 affirming that friendship after Trump retook the White House. The flags of Minnesota, Ontario, both towns, and both countries fly outside the town offices in Fort Frances. But there’s only so much – and really, nothing – that a local official can do to blunt the economic effects of slipshod tariffs put in place by one man, more than a thousand miles away in Washington.

Hoping for the best

Most Canadians recognize this, according to Andrew Hallikas, the mayor of Fort Frances. They like Americans, and Fort Frances residents can relate to Minnesotans a lot: they share similar interests, in the outdoors and in community, he said. But they’re “irate” at Trump – for bullying their country, for going against an ally – and for suggesting Canada should become the 51st US state.

“You cannot imagine how angry that makes us,” Hallikas said. “Please quote me on this. I cannot make this clear enough: we will never become the 51st state. We consider ourselves to probably be the best country in the world in which to live, and we’re quite content to remain that way, thank you very much.”

For two towns that rely on each other, the tension of the trade war simmers underneath the surface. They all want it to end. They don’t know how, or when, it will.

As the Guardian interviewed the mayor of International Falls at a coffee shop on the town’s main drag, a Fort Frances resident interjected angrily to tell the mayor that Canadians are “so pissed off” at Trump for how he’s attacked their country and that International Falls needed Canadians to survive. Their town was suffering, and their businesses losing longtime customers from Canada, because of it, he said.

“I’m originally from the Falls, but I’m an American living in Canada,” the man said. “I’m scared to put that American flag on my shirt, what he’s done.”

Residents, and the leaders of the towns, are worried about how they will rebuild the relationship between their two countries if this continues for much longer. Businesses will find other suppliers. Shoppers will replace their favorites with homegrown options. The sense of nationalism hardens.

“We just hope for the best at this point,” said the International Falls mayor, Drake Dill.

Grant Hauschild, a Democratic Minnesota state senator who represents 65% of the state’s border with Canada, said he’s heard from businesses that have lost up to 30% of their revenue from Canadians. With people already struggling with inflation and high costs, he said a hit like that goes from “a concern to devastation”.

“My hope is, of course, that the relationship goes back to normal once we pass these chaotic times,” Hauschild said. “I think that’s what really scares me most … Even if people want to go back to the way things were, they might have unfortunately kind of moved on – and moved beyond – the relationship.”

Two towns, one community

To cross the Rainy River into either side, people use a toll bridge, with the cost for an average car now $10. They present documents to customs agents on whichever side they’re entering, and answer questions about their purpose in town. People who cross regularly recognize the agents and ask after their families.

The main parts of each respective town sit on either side of the crossing, with both towns initially growing around paper mills. Fort Frances’ mill has since closed; International Falls’ is still running. Fort Frances is larger than International Falls, and because Canada is more sparse, Fort Frances serves as a regional hub. Its hospital will soon be getting an MRI machine – a huge boon for its aging population.

The shops on either side carry gifts from both countries, catering to tourists who fly in to fish, mostly for walleye, and largely on the Canadian side. In a Fort Frances store, kids books called “Little Minnesota” and “Little Canada” sat right beside each other on a shelf. In International Falls, shelves of souvenir cups carried designs for International Falls and Canada.

While Canadian flags line the shop windows and fly throughout downtown Fort Frances, Hallikas said this is not a reflection of increased patriotism, but just a border town welcoming visitors to their country. The two towns are “neighbors by geography, but we are friends by choice”, he said.

“The bridge is over 100 years old, and we’ve been going back and forth it for over 100 years,” Hallikas said. “Before that, there was a ferry. But our friendship is still going to exist when Trump is long gone.”

Dill, the International Falls mayor, owned a business and lived in Canada for 11 years. Many of his friends are Canadian. This fall, he will go up to an island in Canada to meet up with friends.

“There’s no politics in that. There’s no thought of exchange rate, or trade war, or tariffs. It’s just – we’re friends,” he said. “But then you come home and you talk and you watch the news. … I would be really disappointed if it gets to a point where we can’t work through it, and there’s a fundamental change that will hurt International Falls significantly.”

Residents on both sides have favorite products they grab whenever they cross. For Heather Johnson, executive director of the Fort Frances chamber of commerce, it’s Top the Tater, an iconic Minnesota chive and onion dip. She also checks prices on cheeses, and peruses the wider variety of pastas for sale in US stores. Johnson bowls weekly in a league in International Falls, made up of both Americans and Canadians.

Leanne Guba, a Canadian who owns Hometown Hobby and Crafts in International Falls, crosses back into her home country once or twice a month, usually walking across the bridge, to buy ketchup chips, chocolate bars and Dad’s brand oatmeal chocolate chip cookies.

American liquor is no longer on the shelves at government-run Ontario liquor stores, by order of Premier Doug Ford. The push to buy Canadian is “pretty well elbows-up”, Johnson said. “I’m drinking Canadian red wine now.”

‘Mr T took care of that’

Reid, the duty-free shop owner, said the tourist season was about average for him, with no noticeable decline in sales. He has seen some change in his customers.

A couple of years ago, they’d come in with the signature red Maga (Make America Great Again) hats. Last year, not as many. This year, he didn’t see any red hats, and customers would tell him they didn’t vote for Trump. They’ll ask about the missing American bourbon from his shelves, and he’ll tell them, “Mr T took care of that”.

He used to cross the border to go to a show, or the grocery store, or Menard’s, a hardware store, but not anymore. His daughter and her husband used to cross weekly for a date night and shopping, but no longer. People over here are “really upset” with Trump, he said. It has renewed his sense of Canadian pride, but “I’ve always had good pride”.

Johnson, whose kids are now grown, said: “I’m glad that my kids grew up knowing both countries, and they know that there really isn’t a difference in people.”

Across the border in International Falls, craft store owner Guba said she was seeing fewer Canadians, for several reasons. They’re dealing with rising costs, too, and the exchange rate is unfavorable. Some of it is politics, she said. Canadian regulars are coming less frequently.

“They’re definitely being a little more picky about when they come over or being more careful about what they buy,” she said.

The decline, while dealing with unpredictable tariffs on goods she brings in from overseas, has had an impact on her business. She’s adapted by seeking out new suppliers, bringing in new merchandise lines, and trying to reduce costs. She has a few companies she orders from in Canada – including a toy brand and a puzzle company – and expects the new tariffs will likely increase costs on those products.

People are upset about the political dynamics, but they don’t tend to vent their political frustrations openly, she said. There may be the odd joke here and there, but not usually full-blown political debate. “We tend to try to stay friendly,” she said.

The latest tourist season was “decent”, she said. “Overall, we’re still surviving … You can’t really control it.”

‘We remain neutral’

It’s tough to gauge the full impact of declining Canadian spending in the border town, though anecdotally, people are noticing it. The International Falls chamber of commerce would not comment on the impact of the tariffs on the town, or the deteriorating relationship between the two countries.

“We remain neutral on political matters so that we can best serve our diverse membership, which includes individuals and organizations with a wide range of views. Because of that, the Chamber does not have an official comment on the political issues surrounding the US-Canada relationship,” the chamber said in an email.

Isaac Johnson, who owns the Coffee Landing café in International Falls and lives above it with his wife, said he still sees a lot of Canadians who come over to grab espresso and breakfast. He loves his Canadian customers, including the couple he watched meet up at the coffee shop from across the border. They later married.

The locals are caught in the middle of political games, said Johnson, who tries to just focus on himself, his family, and his faith. But people do get emotional about it at times, and “if you definitely bring up politics, for sure,” he said – just as the man who confronted Dill, the mayor, did.

The man, who didn’t share his name or want to have a longer conversation with a reporter, said he’s noticed far fewer Canadians around town, nothing like it used to be. He described Canadians as “very pissed off” and said snowbirds were selling their houses in the US. International Falls voters went for Trump in 2024.

These broader issues, like the trade war, “pit us against each other”, Johnson said, noting that the man got mad at the mayor “over a guy that’s making billions off us all”.

“I love the Canadians, I love Americans, and I love them coming over here and enjoying what we have here, and we can go and enjoy what they have,” Johnson said.

Dill, the town’s mayor, said Canadians are “definitely” not coming to International Falls as much as they were, though he thinks it has more to do with the exchange rate. Still, he said later, “we need all the Canadian commerce we can get, and I would like to think they feel the same way”.

Local officials are in a tough position. They have no control over the tariffs, though with their communities at the center of the impact, they are expected to answer questions and concerns over levies. They have no direct line to the Trump administration, if that would even make a difference. And their communities are suffering.

Hope springs eternal

Hauschild, the Minnesota state senator, said he meets regularly with the Canadian consulate in St Paul, and reiterates his belief in a strong relationship with Canada. But as a state lawmaker, he has little to no control over any of it, beyond using his bully pulpit.

Hallikas, the Fort Frances mayor, said most Canadians have “no rancor for individual Americans” and treat them kindly when they visit, largely avoiding talking about Trump or American politics. Americans will have to work to undo the damage Trump has done to the relationship between the two countries, and that will take time, even after the trade war simmers down or ends, he said.

“But we’ll still be friends with the folks in Minnesota and International Falls,” Hallikas said.

Dill said he doesn’t often run into the frustrations directed at him by the man in the coffee shop, though it happens. He doesn’t have any way he can directly fix the issue.

“The US elected our current president and he has his own agenda and I don’t see that I can stop it,” he said. “I don’t want it to affect us locally. We’ll see. Hope springs eternal. I mean, I thought that everything was going along fine, but apparently it wasn’t.”

The uncertainty of it all is “frustrating”, and he’s most curious about where it all lands, when a truce could be signed so that businesses can have a sense of comfort in planning for their futures. The two countries are engaged in a heated dispute – or a “donnybrook,” as they would say in Canada, noted Dill.

He likened the current situation to two longtime best friends, who hunted and fished and vacationed together for years – until one of them said, you’ve been taking advantage of me for years.

“That’s like driving a nail in a fence,” he said, “and then you pull it out, and even if the fence still stands, there’s a hole where the nail was.”

articles.title: Spanish Grand Prix result: Kimi Antonelli wins after Lando Norris loses lead because of virtual safety car timing
articles.text:
Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli won the Spanish Grand Prix after McLaren's Lando Norris lost out because of the bad timing of a virtual safety car.

Norris was leading comfortably from pole position when the VSC was called on lap 15. The timing was terrible for the world champion - he had already passed the pit exit when the VSC was called.

That meant Antonelli and Red Bull's Max Verstappen were able to pit under the VSC, saving time, while the caution period ended before Norris could make it around to the pits again.

He did then come in but, to make matters worse, the stop was slow and he rejoined in fifth place.

Norris was able to recover only to third around the new Madring track in Madrid where overtaking is next to impossible.

Antonelli's eighth win in 14 races this year puts an even tighter stranglehold on the championship for the Italian.

He is now 81 points ahead of team-mate George Russell, who finished fifth after a difficult race on a confusing strategy, and 101 clear of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, who retired early on with brake failure.

"It's good to win but it doesn't feel as good because Lando deserved to win," Antonelli said.

Norris said: "We'll take it on the chin. There could be more wins this year."

The key stories of the maiden Madring race were:

Norris' terrible luck with the VSC depriving him of a likely third victory this year after a brilliant pole on Saturday

Antonelli's fortune in a season that is surrendering to him, as well as him grabbing it by the throat with his performances

The difficulty of overtaking on a new track designed from a clean sheet of paper, yet without obvious passing places

Norris knew that holding on to the lead would be tough from pole but he robustly defended from Antonelli into the first corner.

The Mercedes driver cut the chicanes at Turns One and Two, and again at Turns Five and Six, each time getting into the lead, each time having to give it back.

After that, Norris looked to be in control of the race as he extended his advantage progressively, moving 5.6 seconds clear 10 laps in, and 6.2 when Lance Stroll's Aston Martin stopped at Turn 20 with brake failure.

The VSC was called, but Norris had already reached the pit straight, while Antonelli and Verstappen had not and could come in.

Norris came in the next time around, but the VSC ended a couple of corners before he reached the entry to the pits, allowing the cars still on track to get back up to racing speed - a stop under a safety car saves a driver about 10 seconds over one under green-flag conditions.

To make matters worse, McLaren's mechanics had trouble with both the right-hand side wheels, and the stop took seven seconds rather than the usual two.

Norris came out in fifth place, 6.3secs behind Russell, and his hopes of winning were gone.

At the front, Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, who had been running fourth before the VSC, stayed out, having started the race on hard tyres rather than the mediums chosen by Antonelli and Norris and the softs Verstappen had.

Leclerc stayed out, and led the race with Antonelli close behind but the gap fluctuated as the Mercedes driver managed his tyres.

Ferrari kept Leclerc out as long as possible, hoping for a second safety car to enable him to make his own cheap stop.

But one never came, and Leclerc had to pit eventually, on lap 48 with nine to go. He resumed in fourth behind Antonelli, Verstappen and Norris.

Norris had closed all his deficit to Verstappen by the final stages and was running right on the Dutchman's tail in the closing laps, but was unable to pass.

The closest he came was with two laps to go as Verstappen stumbled over some lapped cars, but despite a mistake at Turn Five, the Dutchman was able to hold on.

Officials briefly looked at an incident with two laps to go when he cut a chicane while fighting to stay ahead of Norris, who complained Verstappen should give the place up. But no action was taken.

articles.title: Conor Benn: Two-round defeat by Ryan Garcia in Las Vegas shows British fighter's limitations
articles.text:
On one side of the road, Las Vegas tourists were being turned upside down on the New York-New York Hotel's rollercoaster.

On the other side, the biggest night of Conor Benn's career plummeted into freefall.

The polarising British welterweight arrived at T-Mobile Arena chasing a first world title and vindication after four chaotic years that stretched his reputation, career and resolve almost to breaking point.

But rather than Benn leaving with his mission accomplished, Ryan Garcia laid bare the unforgiving reality of elite-level boxing, taking just two rounds to dismantle, drop and stop the 29-year-old.

The Essex fighter's career has been so consumed by events outside the ring - the failed drugs test and provisional suspension, the WBC's mocked "highly elevated egg consumption" ruling, the Chris Eubank Jr saga and an acrimonious split with Eddie Hearn - that the most basic question of just how good he actually is had become obscured.

"It went kind of exactly how I imagined it. He was going to try and put pressure on me straight away," Garcia said afterwards.

"He was banking on the idea I may just start folding early on and maybe get tired. You can't jump in like that. It's not the move."

Benn was taken to hospital after the fight, in what was understood to be a precautionary measure.

The manner of defeat provided the clearest answer yet about Benn's place in the boxing world order.

It forces a reassessment of the route which brought Benn here, and whether his body of work really suggested he was ready for, or deserving of, a world-title fight.

Benn had not competed at the 10st 7lb welterweight limit for more than four years, with the two defining nights of his career coming at middleweight against Eubank.

His revenge victory in the rematch was impressive, but a points win over faded 37-year-old Regis Prograis in April hardly looked ideal preparation for a fight against Garcia - one of the world's leading welterweights.

Yet such is Benn's commercial pull that the traditional stages of a boxing education have often felt secondary. His surname brings attention given his father's illustrious career, his fighting style guarantees excitement, and the story around him has rarely been anything other than compelling.

Garcia, though, provided something none of those aspects can - an elite examination - and Benn failed it.

Thirty-six years after Nigel Benn stopped Iran Barkley in the opening round in Las Vegas, his son was chasing his own defining night.

As the Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua era moves towards its conclusion, British boxing is increasingly searching for its next crossover star and Benn looked the part in Las Vegas before battle commenced.

He had the swagger, the looks and the tailor-made dress sense. Speaking Spanish during media interviews even helped turn some Mexican boos into cheers.

The Americans bought into the package and Zuffa Boxing leaned heavily into his aura, with Dame Helen Mirren narrating a promotional film charting his rise.

But looking like a world-level star and possessing world-level ability are not the same thing.

Benn entered as the WBC's number one contender and BoxRec's highest-ranked British welterweight despite his inactivity in the division.

British boxing has now been given two uncomfortable reminders about 'levels' in quick succession.

Nobody should begrudge a fighter for accepting a life-changing world-title shot, but bypassing the traditional British, Commonwealth and European route removes learning fights.

Heavyweight Moses Itauma has extraordinary talent but was accelerated towards a world title fight with Filip Hrgovic before his professional education had fully caught up.

Benn's route was different, and Itauma was winning his own showpiece fight last month before being stopped, but the lesson is strikingly similar.

"I think he needs a little bit more patience," Garcia said - almost identical advice to that offered by Hrgovic to Itauma.

Some might argue that 'burst' is too final.

It would be unfair not to credit Benn's in-ring evolution, going from a raw novice who used to take beatings in sparring to becoming one of British boxing's most recognisable fighters.

There will still be major fights available, not least a potential trilogy with Eubank.

But his next decision now carries greater significance.

Benn had said he planned to move up in weight regardless of Saturday's result.

With no rehydration clause, he looked strikingly bigger in the ring and had posted footage on Friday evening suggesting he was 32lb heavier than at the official weigh-in, although the figure was not independently verified.

That inevitably reignites debate around extreme weight cutting, but there is also a more immediate sporting concern. If Benn struggled so badly with Garcia's speed and timing, moving up to face naturally bigger men brings its own dangers.

Zuffa Boxing chief Dana White largely sidestepped that question afterwards.

"Let Conor go home, spend some time with his family, enjoy the success he had this year," White said. "When he's ready to come back and lets us know, we'll figure out what's next for him."

Asked whether moving up against bigger opponents could prove even more dangerous, White said: "We'll see. We'll see how the whole thing figures out."

Benn did not attend the post-fight news conference, leaving White to face questions about a fighter Zuffa reportedly paid £11m to sign for his initial deal.

Asked whether Benn had still been worth the money, White bluntly said: "Every penny of it."

But after Garcia exposed such a sizeable gulf, the road to becoming a world champion suddenly looks considerably longer than it did when he arrived in Las Vegas.

At the weigh-in, Benn said the atmosphere was giving him 'Ricky Hatton in Vegas' vibes, which may have been one of the more optimistic claims of fight week.

English accents were difficult to pick out around the fight venue and whatever travelling support he did have was comprehensively drowned out by Garcia's largely Mexican-American following.

Benn's relationship with the British public remains complicated.

Some boxing supporters still want answers about his two positive tests for clomifene in 2022. Benn has always denied knowingly taking a banned substance and repeatedly said he had evidence to support his innocence, but much of it was never placed into the public domain.

The WBC's conclusion that a "highly elevated consumption of eggs" provided a reasonable explanation for one adverse finding handed his rivals permanent ammunition. Eubank slapped Benn with an egg; Garcia ate one at Thursday's news conference.

There was obvious irony given Garcia's own positive test and subsequent suspension for ostarine in 2024. The Californian also denies knowingly taking performance-enhancing drugs.

Other fighters have managed to move the conversation on by producing defining performances in the ring.

Benn had the chance to do that in Las Vegas. He couldn't take it.

articles.title: US Open 2026 results: Elena Rybakina on title win after pre-tournament injury
articles.text:
Elena Rybakina arrived in New York unable to walk without pain after injuring her foot. She leaves the city as the US Open champion and new world number one.

Kazakhstan's Rybakina produced a brilliant performance to beat two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka 6-4 5-7 6-2 in Saturday's final and repeat her Australian Open success against the same player in January.

Clutching the trophy on Saturday night, Rybakina reflected that "some magic is happening" for her after her difficult lead-in to the tournament.

The 27-year-old aggravated a foot injury during her quarter-final in Cincinnati against Iga Swiatek last month, a little over a week before the final major of the year began.

Playing on through injury could have had dire consequences for the rest of her season - but Rybakina, knowing the top ranking was in her grasp, wanted to try and play in the final Grand Slam of the year.

"I was so upset. I didn't know actually how it was going to be day by day," she said.

"We arrived in New York and did an MRI. It didn't look that great.

"I couldn't even walk for the next few days without pain.

"I was lucky enough to have a very good doctor in Australia. She was on the phone with us all the time and somehow, with the team, we made a plan."

Rybakina did not do any on-court training for a week, but daily recovery sessions in the gym - plus trips for dinner and to the cinema to "switch the mind" - helped get her ready for another major triumph.

She won her first four matches at Flushing Meadows without dropping a set, including seeing off four-time major winner Naomi Osaka.

Her run from then on - which included beating Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen in the quarter-finals, outlasting third seed Coco Gauff in the semis and outplaying top seed Sabalenka in the final - was nothing short of outstanding.

"I was so unlucky with the injury, but I'm very proud," Rybakina said.

"I still can't believe it."

Rybakina had already been confirmed as world number one by reaching the semi-finals in New York. The fact that her final opponent was Sabalenka, the player she will replace at the top of the rankings, added an extra dimension to Saturday's championship match.

Rybakina won the first set despite her serve, one of her biggest weapons, misfiring.

She landed only 27% of her first serves during the opener, but still won 22 of 30 points behind her serve and did not face a break point as she took the lead.

Sabalenka eventually broke in the 12th game of the second set to send their match the distance, but it was Rybakina who dominated the decider.

While her Belarusian opponent grew visibly more frustrated as the final slipped away, Rybakina remained remarkably composed.

"The way she [Rybakina] quietly walks around, she doesn't really lift her head up and she gives no emotion away whatsoever," former British number one Annabel Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Rybakina is like a machine out there. You never know what's going on in her head."

However, nerves did show when Rybakina threw in two double faults as she served for the title.

At 40-30, the trophy in her sights, Rybakina could have blinked. Instead, she coolly sent down her 12th ace of the match to secure her third Grand Slam title.

The second seed produced her biggest celebration of her three major wins - a smile and both arms raised in celebration as she took in the applause.

Rybakina has now won two of her three Grand Slam finals against Sabalenka, all of which have come on their favoured hard courts.

On Monday, Rybakina will become the 30th different women to top the world rankings.

She is a different personality to Sabalenka, who held the position for the past 99 weeks, but Croft believes she will "take it in her stride".

"I actually think she has the right personality to deal with it," Croft said.

"There are going to be a lot of players around her nipping at her heels. She can fluctuate with her levels, but when it really matters, we've seen her be able to bring it to the table.

"It's not going to be easy to hang on to it. I think women's tennis is really exciting right now."

Rybakina has completed three parts of the career Grand Slam, with just a French Open victory missing from her collection.

After winning Wimbledon in 2022, she did not claim her second major until January's Australian Open, and has now added a third in New York.

She has never previously been further than the quarter-finals at Roland Garros, although she did win a WTA 1,000 event on clay in Rome in 2023.

Former British number one Laura Robson said on Sky Sports: "She is an all-surface player - clay is the worst one, but when you get her on something that's quite lively or quick, she's unplayable at times.

"I genuinely think she will win many more Slams. I just don't see, when her serve and return are on, how pretty much anyone can beat her on a hard court."

articles.title: US Open 2026 final: Alexander Zverev and Ben Shelton emerge from shadows of Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz
articles.text:
For different reasons, Alexander Zverev and Ben Shelton will look back on their 2026 Grand Slam performances with a sense of achievement - no matter what happens in Sunday's US Open men's final.

German top seed Zverev has emerged from the shadow of Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz to win the Grand Slam title many felt he might never land.

American eighth seed Shelton, meanwhile, has demonstrated he does have what it takes to reach a major final - and beat the world's very best players on the way.

"For me, this whole tournament has been uncharted territory," said Shelton, who will be backed by a partisan 24,000-strong crowd in New York.

"I'm in positions I've never been in before. I've beaten guys I've never beaten before."

Shelton must also beat Zverev for the first time, having lost all five of their previous meetings, if he is to become the first American man in 23 years to win a Grand Slam singles title.

At the start of the season, the odds on Zverev winning two Grand Slam titles would have been long. They are considerably shorter now.

The French Open champion is a slight favourite to beat Shelton as he looks to double his tally of major wins - not only for the year, but his career.

After three defeats in major finals, many thought the 29-year-old had missed his chance to win one of the sport's biggest prizes given how Sinner and Alcaraz - who swept the Grand Slams in 2024 and 2025 and together earned the 'Sincaraz' tag - have dominated.

But injuries to the standout pair - Alcaraz missing the French Open and Wimbledon, with Sinner ruled out of the US Open - have opened the door for someone else to make a push.

Asked if he thought he could end 2026 with more major wins than them, Zverev said: "I believed in it. I believed that it's possible. I think not many of you guys did.

"I think the question was always: Is Carlos and Jannik going to play all four Grand Slam finals between each other again?

"Of course, it was a very legit question with how the last two years went. I'm happy with how this year went so far, but I've got another big match on Sunday."

Zverev is contesting his second US Open final, having squandered a two-set lead against Dominic Thiem in 2020 - a gutting defeat that cut deep.

In the seasons that followed, Zverev often played in the latter stages at Slams with the demeanour of a man who lacked belief that his time would ever come.

His mental misgivings were finally put to bed by beating Italy's Flavio Cobolli in the final at Roland Garros and, after finishing runner-up to Sinner at Wimbledon, he has now reached a third successive Grand Slam final.

A below-par Zverev ground through the opening rounds at Flushing Meadows in a series of early-morning finishes, but he gradually improved over a fortnight where he has not yet faced a top-20 opponent.

Shelton will present a considerable step up in quality but, like Cobolli, is another opponent who may feel the weight of occasion too difficult to bear.

The significance of reaching a first US Open final has not escaped Shelton's notice.

Shelton, 23, is bidding to become the first home US Open men's singles champion since Andy Roddick in 2003 and could also become the first black American man to win a singles major since Arthur Ashe in 1975.

When a reporter said after his semi-final win over Frances Tiafoe that there was a "lot of history" on the line, a grinning Shelton replied: "Is there?"

Former world number four James Blake believes a Shelton win would be huge for African-American representation in the sport.

"Having another black American in the final leaves you wondering how many kids and adults are watching that maybe wouldn't have been otherwise," Blake told BBC Sport.

"They are going to be inspired to hear Ben's story and see someone that looks like them out there playing and competing in a sport that has historically been dominated by the sense of a country club white sport."

Known for a thunderous serve which has topped 140mph over the past fortnight, Shelton has complemented his attacking instincts by developing his defensive skills and improving his weaker backhand.

Shelton's progress has led to four title victories this season - Dallas (indoor hard), Munich (clay), Stuttgart (grass) and Canadian Open (outdoor hard) - and a watershed win over Alcaraz at the US Open.

Shelton had never beaten a top-three opponent until overcoming the seven-time champion, who was playing in his first tournament for almost five months, in an epic quarter-final which ended at 3:34am.

"Ben has been trending in the right direction throughout this year. I think four titles on different surfaces is evidence of it," Shelton's father and coach Bryan said.

"He's willing to suffer a little bit in the rallies, go deeper and really use his athleticism."

articles.title: South Africa v New Zealand: What did we learn from Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series?
articles.text:
South Africa further cemented themselves as the world's best team with a 3-1 victory over New Zealand in the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series.

After losing the opening Test in Johannesburg, the world champions won three straight games, comfortably claiming the series with a 43-28 win in Baltimore.

The fourth Test, played in the United States, came after three Tests in South Africa where the All Blacks continued to show promising signs under Dave Rennie.

With the Rugby World Cup next year, what did we learn from the series, which replaced this year's Rugby Championship and will be played again in 2029?

New Zealander Tony Brown's arrival as attack coach in 2024 pointed to South Africa's ambition to dominate in all facets of the game.

The former Highlanders head coach, who will join the All Blacks in 2028, is known for creating a cohesive attacking shape built on sharp ball movement.

But having been outscored in terms of tries over the first two Tests, the Springboks flipped their pack-power trump card - pivotal to their back-to-back World Cup successes - to prevent a repeat of New Zealand's victorious 1996 series win in South Africa.

Nothing illustrated that more than a monster maul that started just inside New Zealand's 22 and ended with Malcolm Marx peeling off to score the decisive try under the posts.

That came after a penalty try from a scrum in the first half. In Baltimore, their power again proved too much.

"South Africa have tried to play expansively a couple of times when we have dominance after hurting teams in the maul or scrum," Schalk Brits, a 2019 World Cup winner, told BBC Sport.

"New Zealand didn't have that dominance in the forwards, but people said they played beautiful rugby. I don't care if it is beautiful or not.

"Beauty is in the eye of the beholder and I love a maul and scrum."

Fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, who was injured at the end of May, returned to start all four Tests. He was initially named on the bench for the second match, only for Handre Pollard to withdraw.

Despite improving as the series went on, the 24-year-old lacked his usual flashes of individual brilliance.

It remains to be seen whether South Africa turn back to 32-year-old Pollard, as they did in 2023, on the biggest occasions to close out games.

Rassie Erasmus' experienced back-to-back World Cup winners - Marx (32), Eben Etzebeth (34), Pieter-Steph du Toit (34), Siya Kolisi (35), Damian de Allende (34), Cheslin Kolbe (32) - all remain regular starters.

The world champions have proven they can also play an exciting brand of attacking rugby, but appeasing the masses will not matter if a familiar formula can bring them three straight World Cups.

Scott Robertson's dismissal in January after two years as head coach sunk New Zealand to a new low.

Rennie, not the flashiest appointment, had to hit the ground running, and a stunning Test win over South Africa at Ellis Park was a case of doing just that.

The 33-16 victory injected jeopardy into a series which many had the Springboks winning comfortably, given their home advantage and recent dominance.

Hurricanes half-backs Cam Roigard and Ruben Love, both aged 25, were trusted by Rennie to instil a return to the All Blacks way - the ability to score from transition from anywhere on the field and compound scoreboard pressure.

Four or more tries in each Test in South Africa showed just that, with the third Test all square at half-time.

"Scott Robertson was a good culture coach but maybe not a brilliant technical coach. Dave Rennie is a brilliant technical coach," former England wing Ugo Monye told Rugby Union Weekly.

"After the Nations Championship, you could see the structures and how they want to play. I think the All Blacks' backline is the most skilled in World Rugby."

Love struggled to have the same commanding impact in Tests two and three, with fly-half Richie Mo'unga returning for the Baltimore game, his first Test since the World Cup final.

The 32-year-old Mo'unga, who is back after a stint in Japan, was not at the standard that made him one of the best fly-halves at the 2023 World Cup.

However, getting him back up to speed will be an All Blacks goal over the next 12 months.

Former England scrum-half Danny Care said: "Imagine what New Zealand would do with a platform and some dominance. It is great for the game that they are coming back to be the All Blacks of old, and the next 12 months will be fascinating."

South Africa live for must-win games. That is when, according to Brits, the Boks "come alive".

Defeat at Ellis Park cost them their world number one status - which was quickly regained - but also exposed a vulnerability.

South Africa, who lost matches in the pool stages of the past two World Cups, are currently the favourites to win next year's tournament in Australia, bringing a pressure they have not experienced previously.

"We hate being the favourite, we almost have to have our backs against the wall," Brits said.

"We prefer not to have the eyes on us and move under the radar. I think that is the best way for any team."

Back-to-back Six Nations champions France sent a weakened side to Christchurch in July and lost 34-32 to New Zealand.

When matched against the Springboks last November, France were beaten emphatically, 32-17.

Brits believes France are "the most settled" and offer tactical flexibility similar to that of the world champions.

"I feel like South Africa have an advantage as they can play multiple styles, and it feels like most other nations don't have that capability," Brits said.

"The only team that can play multiple styles is France, as they can grind it out with the forwards, play the kicking game and the expansive game as well."

He added that England still need to become what they are "supposed to be" and to keep an eye on Ireland, who are travelling "under the radar" after peaking in previous World Cup cycles prior to the tournament.

"Ireland still have amazing rugby players and coaches – the best coaches out there - and a top-four squad," Brits added. "Be careful of Ireland."

articles.title: England cricket: Test opener may not have to be specialist amid Gay, Bethell & Cox debate - Trescothick
articles.text:
England's Test opener does not necessarily have to be a specialist at the top of the order, according to Marcus Trescothick.

England have a decision to make over how to accommodate Jacob Bethell when he returns from a knee injury for the tour of South Africa in December.

Emilio Gay, in his first summer as a Test cricketer, has opened alongside Ben Duckett. Gay has made three half-centuries, though he ends the season with an average below 25.

Duckett, one of England's senior players, made the team's only century of the summer, against New Zealand at Trent Bridge in June. However, the 31-year did not reach 20 in the three-match series against Pakistan and averages less than 24 since the beginning of the Ashes.

Jordan Cox has impressed as Bethell's replacement at number three. After finally making his debut this summer, Cox has averaged more than 42 and opened in first-class cricket early in his career.

Bethell has been touted as a potential opener and has moved up to open in England's one-day team.

The other new member of England's top six for the Pakistan series, Dan Lawrence, may be exempt from conversations over who is squeezed out because of the off-spin he offers, though Bethell's return would also bring some left-arm spin.

Trescothick has been England's interim coach for the Pakistan series and will now hand the reins to New Zealander Stephen Fleming, who is due to travel to the UK in the coming days to begin planning for the trip to South Africa.

"You generally want your best top seven, however that looks," said Trescothick. "Who that's going to be, I don't know. That's for someone else to work out."

Trescothick is one of England's most successful Test openers and was part of the team that famously won the 2005 Ashes. The former Somerset man believes the game is different to when he ended his 76-Test career in 2006.

"I reckon times have changed a little bit," said the 50-year-old. "I think you look at your best batting line-up, however that fits up.

"If that's with a specialist opener, great. If not, I think you can plan around it in this day and age. Players adapt pretty quickly because they're chopping and changing formats."

Fleming was appointed England's new Test coach in July, yet he missed the 3-0 series win against Pakistan.

The former New Zealand captain will now arrive for meetings with the England hierarchy.

He is expected to watch some of England's white-ball series against Sri Lanka, with the ODI and T20 teams still led by Fleming's fellow Kiwi and good friend Brendon McCullum. Fleming could also visit some of the counties.

When McCullum was in charge of both the Test and white-ball teams, he kept the same backroom team across formats, including Trescothick as an assistant.

However, it now looks likely that the staff will be reorganised. Former Australia batter Mike Hussey said he was approached by Fleming, though it has been reported down under that Hussey has declined.

Trescothick said he has not got clarity on his future role. He confirmed he has a preference but declined to reveal it.

"It's probably best I don't mention it at the moment because it may not be the case of what happens," he said. "I love doing both formats. It's brilliant and I've been privileged to be in the position of assistant coach."

Trescothick will be joined on England's staff by former team-mate Kevin Pietersen, who has been appointed as a consultant for the white-ball team.

Pietersen, one of the most flamboyant and innovative batters to play for England, returns to the national team 12 years after he was effectively sacked following the 5-0 Ashes defeat in 2013-14.

The 46-year-old's first day back in the England set-up is on Sunday, joining preparations for the first T20 against Sri Lanka in Southampton on Tuesday.

"We've spoken already, to plan a little bit," said Trescothick. "I gave him a couple of things that I wanted him to look at, to get his advice on.

"He is buzzing. Putting back on the shirt or the tracksuit, he is buzzing for that opportunity.

"Having his presence around and the knowledge he has about batting – he sees batting in a different light to many different people. If we can tap into that, it's only going to benefit the team."

articles.title: Manchester United v Manchester City: Premier League – live
articles.text:
13 min Quite a cagey start overall. Erling Haaland is yet to touch the ball.

11 min Cunha breaks into space from midfield, only to drag a miserable long-range shot well wide. He had better options right and certainly left.

11 min Mbeumo is flattened by Anderson, who looks a bit manic and is probably one foul away from a yellow card.

9 min After a slow start, United are starting to get on the ball. Fernandes clips a teasing pass over the defence towards Dalot, who makes a terrific run infield but can’t control the ball in mid-air. Had he done so, he would have had a shooting chance. But it would have been a tough ball for Diego Maradona to kill, never mind Diogo Dalot.

Updated at 11.41 EDT

7 min The resulting free-kick is taken on the right by Fernandes and retrieved on the far side by Rashford. He finds the supporting Martinez, who sweeps a left-foot shot from 25 yards; Donnarumma makes a comfortable save.

Updated at 11.38 EDT

6 min Rashford stays down holding his head after being sandwiched by Semenyo and Anderson. I think he was accidentally caught by Anderson as he fell.

Either way, he’s fine to continue.

Updated at 11.38 EDT

5 min Anderson’s first corner is headed behind for another. It’s taken short and worked across the field to Cherki on the right. His floated cross is eventually lumped clear by Dorgu.

3 min City have started well. Foden plays a perfectly timed lay off to Enzo Fernandez, whose shot from 20 yards hits Maguire and ricochets behind for a corner.

2 min And, as expected, Antoine Semenyo has started on the left for City with Phil Foden on the right.

Maguire chops Cherki down 40 yards from goal – a challenge which, in the opinion of Gary Neville on Sky, might have brought a yellow card had it not been so early in the contest.

Updated at 11.33 EDT

1 min United kick off from left to right as we watch. Sounds like a cracking atmosphere at Old Trafford.

United have started with Cunha as their false nine. No funny stuff from Michael Carrick.

“Manchester Utd have to be physical,” writes AnhTuan Nguyen Huynh. “With Benjamin Sesko on the bench, City won.”

I’d politely – nay, meekly – disagree. I think they need pace on the counter-attack for the first hour. Sesko is rapid but I don’t know whether his movement in transition is as good as the other options. I suspect, had Amad Diallo been fit, United would have started Mbeumo up front. They may yet do that, with Cunha roaming from the right.

Match report: Coventry 0-5 Brighton

The bare statistic is bleak: Coventry City are only the second team in Premier League history to lose their first four games of the season without scoring in any of them. “And yet …” will be the enduring message from Frank Lampard.

And yet they have caused problems for opposition teams – even at points when down to 10 men here against Brighton. And yet they have already faced three of the top flight’s European contingent. And yet they are not playing that badly. But they simply cannot find the point, or even the goal, that would give their confidence a much-needed boost. And it does not take long for a promoted club’s relegation fears to turn realistic.

Enzo Maresca’s pre-match thoughts

double quotation mark[What’s the key on derby day?] Probably to keep the emotion away, but that’s not easy. Embrace the chaos – it’s a derby, it’s nice – and try to play our game.

I’m happy because we have different options [on the bench]. He [Ayyoub Bouaddi] played very well against Porto and is going to bring up a lot of happiness.

Man Utd’s tactics Given the success of Bryan Mbeumo up front against City last season, there’s a case for United starting with Matheus Cunha on the left and the speedier Marcus Rashford up front. We’ll see.

Some more pre-match reading

If you’re a Manchester United fan, or just a fan of great writing, I heartily recommend United Writing, a Substack written by my colleague (and mentor) Tim de Lisle. Here’s the latest piece on Sabah, Youri Tielemans and more.

Brighton’s fourth goal was a screamer from Lewis Dunk, of all people, prompting this email from Steve Bradfield.

double quotation markIs Brighton’s fourth goal a slam Dunk for goal of month?

Full time: Coventry 0-5 Brighton

Brighton are up to fourth after hammering the bottom club Coventry, who remain stuck on nil points and nil goals.

Will Unwin, our man at Old Trafford, says the pre-match protests were “not as vociferous and well attended as previous protests”. Especially this one.

Enzo Maresca has backed Elliot Anderson’s assessment that ­Manchester City are the “kings of Manchester” as he prepares for his first derby in charge of the club.

City travel to Old Trafford seeking to continue their perfect start to life under Maresca and further prove Anderson’s point. The 23-year-old midfielder made his claim on signing from Nottingham Forest for £116m in the summer and having witnessed City win eight Premier League titles during the past 14 years, compared with United’s one.

“I think Manchester City was unbelievable what they achieved. It’s normal when Elliot said that,” said Maresca. “If you go back it’s a different picture, but for me the reason he said that is because when he grew up Manchester City was dominant.”

Premier League latest: Coventry 0-3 Brighton “Feel free to just gloss over the other game today,” writes Eddy Nason. “Clearly nothing happening there (uncovers eyes to check how bad it’s getting).”

Yeah sorry, I’m not sure why we’re not covering that. But it’s a case of grim and grimmer for Coventry fans: their team are 3-0 down after 76 minutes and Taiwo Awoniyi has been sent off.

It was a sight the England press pack became increasingly used to seeing after the team’s World Cup matches over the summer. Kobbie Mainoo was invariably the first to leave the dressing room, walk through the mixed zone – eyes dead ahead, features impassive – and board the bus.

It was as if he could not get out of the stadiums quick enough and the further England progressed the more pronounced it started to feel. There was a real gap between Mainoo and the next England player to depart the stadium in the knockout rounds. The Manchester United midfielder is inscrutable, even in the heat of battle. It is part of his enviably unflappable temperament. It was no great leap to imagine what lay behind the mask – tremendous frustration as Thomas Tuchel kept on leaving him out.

Mainoo did not play a single minute at the tournament. He was an unused substitute all the way to the semi-final exit against Argentina, and when everyone expected to see him in the third-place playoff against France he did not make the bench. The Football Association said before the game he had picked up an unspecified injury.

For Mainoo it was a lost summer and yet it was physically and mentally draining all the same, what with the training and travel; the demand to stay focused as he waited and waited. .

United are without Luke Shaw, who has an unspecified injury, so Patrick Dorgu starts at left-back. So much for Michael Carrick repeating his tactics from the win over City in January; on that day Dorgu started as the left-sided attacker and scored the second goal. Dorgu for Shaw is the only change from United’s last Premier League game, the 2-2 draw with Everton a week ago.

Enzo Maresca makes two changes from Manchester City’s win over Coventry last weekend. Matheus Nunes replaces Abdukodir Khusanov at right-back; Phil Foden is preferred to Iliman Ndiaye in attack, which may mean a switch from right to left for Antoine Semenyo. The usual left-winger, Jeremy Doku, is still out with a calf injury.

Man Utd (4-2-3-1) Lammens; Dalot, Maguire, Martinez, Dorgu; Mainoo, Tielemans; Mbeumo, B Fernandes, Rashford; Cunha.

Subs: Andrey Santos, Darlow, Heaven, Lacey, Mazraoui, Mount, Sesko, Yoro, Zirkzee.

Man City (4-2-3-1) Donnarumma; Nunes, Dias, Guehi, Gvardiol; Anderson, Fernandez; Foden, Cherki, Semenyo; Haaland

Subs: Rulli, Ndiaye, Kovacic, Reis, Bouaddi, O’Reilly, Allan, Khusanov, Lewis.

Referee Michael Oliver.

Updated at 11.29 EDT

Manchester City have enjoyed a perfect start to the season without ever looking fully convincing in their victories. There are certainly more positives than negatives as Enzo Maresca learns more and more about his team. Against Porto they were sloppy for far too long and the midfield continues to look open, so a statement performance against their fiercest rivals would be ideal. The quality to rip open a team that has conceded two in each of their three Premier League outings thus far is there, and if it all finally clicks, then it could be a fine day for City.

Michael Carrick is in a not dissimilar position but only has four points to show for United’s indifferent efforts. There is always an underlying pressure for any Manchester United and he faces difficult league games today and next weekend at Fulham before an elongated international break. He can’t afford two defeats because there will be a long silence that will be filled with think pieces on the club because it is impossible to escape the noise at this club.

Manchester United’s nine victories from 10 Premier League games at Old Trafford in 2026 cast their stadium as a fortress Manchester City aim to ransack on Sunday, to join Leeds in departing with three points during this calendar year.

Michael Carrick has overseen the division’s highest home points-per-game return in that span: 2.7, ahead of Arsenal’s 2.27 (from 12 matches) and Manchester City’s 2.25 (11); and his side have scored the most goals: 26, to City’s 23, and the champions’ 20.

A United fan group, the 1958, has called for a “peaceful protest” before kick-off, starting at a pub near the stadium, against what it believes is disproportionate action in the club’s drive to eradicate ticket touting. United said on Friday that 685 accounts had been subject to a ban and 464 supporters had received a reduced sanction or final warning.

Can you have a must-win game in September? How about a mustn’t-lose match? This Manchester derby feels close to the latter for United, who have made a false start to Michael Carrick’s first season as full-time manager and already trail City by five points.

It’s not all doom and gloom for United. They’ve scored nine goals in two home games, and their form at Old Trafford since Carrick took over has been terrific. They’ve won 10 out of 11, including a rousing 2-0 demolition of City in his first match back in January. United counter-attacked to devastating effect in that game; a degree in rocket science is not required to work out Carrick’s tactics today.

City have recovered well after being battered by Arsenal in the Community Shield. You can’t ask for more than three league wins from three, even if the fixtures have been relatively kind. For both sides, this should be a useful health check.

Kick off 4.30pm.

articles.title: Arch Manning leads Texas back from 20 points down in fourth quarter to shock No 1 Ohio State
articles.text:
Arch Manning delivered a moment, and it was a big one for Texas and himself. The Longhorns quarterback led No 4 Texas back from a 20-point fourth-quarter deficit to beat No 1 Ohio State 24-23 on Saturday night.

Using his legs to keep drives going and his right arm to start the rally with a touchdown pass to Ryan Wingo, Manning delivered the kind of primetime performance that could redefine his career and propel the program’s national championship hopes.

“His grit started it,” Texas coach Steve Sarkisian said.

Grit that earned a piece of history. The Longhorns’ 20-point comeback in the fourth quarter is the largest fourth-quarter rally to win against an AP No 1 team, according to Sportradar.

Grit born out of the adversity of last season’s failures. Texas started last season No 1, lost at Ohio State and were soon unranked after a 3-2 start. Manning was the lightning rod for criticism because of erratic play in his first season as the full-time starter.

“Last September was a hard month for him,” Sarkisian said. “I think him getting through the adversity of last year helped him get through the adversity of tonight. When he comes back, everybody else comes back. That’s a guy who has some grit, some resilience.”

Saturday night initially looked like last season’s version of Manning and the Longhorns. His first pass was a completion that was fumbled away. Four plays later, a long throw turned into a fluke interception that set up Ohio State’s first touchdown and a 10-0 Buckeyes lead.

Nothing was working until Texas were backed up near their own end zone in the third quarter and losing 23-3. Manning took a big hit on the sideline as he made a desperate scramble. The hit seemed to wake up the entire offense. He completed 11 of his final 15 passes, directing three scoring drives of 12 plays or longer. Hollywood Smothers finished two of them with short touchdown runs, the last one with just 25 seconds left.

“It was a weird start,” Manning said. “I’m really proud of the way we responded. We could have let that thing go. It’s a testament to our coaches and our culture.”

Manning’s final stat line of 23-of-37 passing for 196 yards and a touchdown won’t light up a Heisman Trophy ballot. But pulling out the win in a game between two national championship contenders shows how far Manning has come as a competitor.

“We just had to get something going. I always knew we were going to be in it in the end,” Manning said. “I’m so glad we won.”

articles.title: AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC
articles.text:
An artificial intelligence researcher who quit AI firm Anthropic has said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

"I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.

Jacob Coxon was speaking to the BBC after his resignation post on the dangers of AI went viral on a backdrop of growing safety concerns about the industry.

The 27-year-old's former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, recently called for AI development to slow down - though some have questioned the motivations behind this.

The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.

Amodei wrote in an essay on Saturday that developing the technology was not in question, but the risks associated with it were "serious", and that companies and governments must be given time to address them.

Coxon – who worked at OpenAI before joining Anthropic – welcomed the suggestion of a slowdown but said it would need to be co-ordinated with China to avoid "a race at an international scale".

"The people who work at these companies are completely serious when they ask for regulation because they find themselves trapped in a race. And they're scared of the outcomes of that race," he told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.

The hardest question to answer, according to Coxon, was what an AI apocalypse would look like.

One of the risks outlined in Amodei's comments was of a swarm of bots acting like a supercomputer that could take over the internet.

Coxon said this scenario could be realistic in six months to a year.

In response to Coxon's departure, an Anthropic spokesperson told BBC News: "We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks.

"To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry."

The firm has been a pioneer in studying how AI models work, the spokesperson added. It was the first to publish a framework for mitigating the risks posed by their development - and it also "aggressively" tests its models and publishes the findings to aid scrutiny and prevent incidents of "AI misalignment".

"This work is also why we believe the world would benefit from the industry adopting a lawful, verifiable way to work together to pace how we release powerful models," they said.

Coxon said his peers feared the danger could even arrive in the next two years.

He said staff at AI firms were "planning what to do with their lives and thinking about the impacts of their work", while some were "considering buying land somewhere because they're so scared of the instability as a result of rapid AI progress".

"They all keep this in their head on a daily basis while working on the technology."

But Coxon did have some optimism about the future of AI, telling the BBC that the people researching the technology "genuinely want to see the upside" of things like "solving diseases and improving everyone's lives".

Many others in the industry have also voiced their concerns since Coxon's social media post, including Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger.

"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," Hubinger said.

Computer scientist and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI", told the BBC on Friday that a 10% chance of AI killing all humans was "not unreasonable", external.

Meanwhile, Marc Warner, chief executive of AI safety firm Faculty, told the BBC's The World This Weekend that it was "extremely hard to place a probability" on AI killing all humans.

"But it's important to recognise that these people are very sincere in what they're saying," he added, noting that the risks surrounding AI have been raised by the heads of several AI firms for years.

Former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, who is a paid adviser to Anthropic, wrote in the Sunday Times, external that he too was worried about the risk of AI to humanity despite generally being optimistic.

However, some industry figures have suggested comments are overstated or may be designed to generate hype.

Chief executive of the AI platform Hugging Face, Clement Delangue, said on social media: "Sorry, but asking Jacob [Coxon] about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change. Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective."

After Amodei's essay was published, however, Delangue offered to help be a part of the potential solutions the Anthropic boss proposed.

Grindr chief executive George Arison expressed similar views when talking to the BBC, suggesting Anthropic and others statements were being made to drum up investor support.

"Because the only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work,'" he said.

Jensen Huang, boss on AI chip maker Nvdia, also discussed Coxon's comments at a conference hosted by the investment bank Goldman Sachs last week, multiple people in the group told the BBC. They said he dismissed them as untrue.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump told reporters on Sunday that the US was "leading China in AI... And frankly, I want to keep it that way. Because whoever wins AI wins".

Other critics say Anthropic has been trying to trigger a regulatory push to block competition, leaving it and OpenAI in a duopoly.

Anthropic is reportedly preparing for a potentially record-setting initial public offering on the stock market, allowing people to buy shares in its firm.

OpenAI, which was most recently valued at $852bn (£630bn), had been expected to do the same, but OpenAI's Altman said on Friday this would not happen this year, citing AI safety concerns.

articles.title: Insider warnings over AI fall flat with some in Silicon Valley
articles.text:
Each September, a who's who of executives from across Silicon Valley descends on San Francisco's Palace Hotel to charm investors at a conference hosted by the investment bank Goldman Sachs.

This past week, between talk of growth and potential returns, tech titans found themselves addressing the abrupt resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon.

Coxon, a 27-year-old who worked at OpenAI before joining its chief rival Anthropic, said on Tuesday that people building artificial intelligence (AI) believed the technology could destroy humanity.

They are "gambling with our lives", he said, "these will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything".

Coxon is by no means the first AI insider to publicly sound the alarm. There have been a string of high-profile resignations from both Anthropic and OpenAI in recent years over apparent safety concerns, and some current Anthropic employees even echoed Coxon's post.

"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," a team lead at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, posted on X.

While Coxon said explicitly in his posts that his warnings were "not marketing", some executives and investors in Silicon Valley have reacted with scepticism to a recent flurry of insiders sounding the alarm.

Anthropic and OpenAI are reportedly preparing for potentially record-setting initial public offerings, and some in the tech sector have suggested the latest stark comments about the dangers of AI may be designed to generate hype by signalling the power of these products.

Anthropic's boss, Dario Amodei, has come under fire for saying AI technology could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs and will "test who we are as a species".

One conference speaker, Grindr chief executive George Arison, told the BBC he believed this week's comments from Coxon and others were indicative of an "anti-civilisational worldview at Anthropic".

He called them "dangerous" and said they had prompted him to instruct some engineers at the LGBTQ+ dating app to stop using Anthropic's technology.

"It is irresponsible for us as stewards of our shareholders' money to be relying on a business that does what this company does, in terms of its public statements," he said.

"Maybe they actually believe it," Arison said. "Or you could argue they're saying it because it's a great way to gin up more investor support, because the only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work.'"

Anthropic was valued at $965bn (£713bn) in its most recent fundraising round earlier this year.

The BBC has asked Anthropic for a response to the statements.

In an essay posted early on Saturday, Amodei called for a slowing of AI model development and global regulation - and said the risks associated with AI were "serious".

Nvidia boss Jensen Huang also discussed Coxon's comments before a crowd at the conference, multiple people in the group told the BBC. They said he dismissed them as untrue.

Huang has previously said the notion that AI "is going to be the end of humanity" is "complete nonsense".

And while he may have a business interest in an AI boom - Nvidia builds chips that power AI systems - his comments reflect a growing backlash in Silicon Valley to the existential warnings from current and former staffers.

Some critics have even accused Anthropic of fearmongering in hopes that it will trigger a regulatory push that could shut out competition and leave it and OpenAI with a duopoly in the sector.

Brad Gerstner, who is the head of the investment firm Altimeter Capital, posted pictures of Huang from the conference and accused Coxon of "ridiculous hyperbole".

On Friday, chief executive of AI platform Hugging Face, Clement Delangue, weighed in. Hugging Face, which Nvidia announced it would acquire last week, was hacked by OpenAI agents earlier this year prompting an outcry over AI safety.

"Sorry, but asking Jacob about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change," he wrote on X. "Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective."

Both Gerstner and Delangue were more circumspect on Saturday after Amodei's proposal was posted, with Gerstner calling the idea "an important step forward" in balancing competing considerations like speed and safety.

Delangue offered to help be a part of the potential solutions proposed by Amodei.

Federal legislation co-sponsored this month by left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, known as the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, would impose a temporary pause in advanced AI development.

"There is a good chance that human beings will lose control over AI," Sanders told the BBC's Newsnight programme on Thursday. "And what happens then, nobody knows. But could it be catastrophic? Yes, it could."

"When scientists tell you there is a chance that it could have a cataclysmic impact on humanity, you've got be a moron not to say, slow it down," he added.

If an industry-wide government crackdown comes, however, it is likely to be led by legislators and not the Trump administration which largely supports a policy of unfettered AI development. It has framed this as necessary to ensure the US does not cede dominance to China.

Speaking to reporters this week, President Donald Trump was asked if he had any concerns about AI leading to human extinction. "No, I don't have any," he said. "I have concerns that if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position. We are leading China right now."

But the president's relationship with Anthropic has been turbulent. After the company refused to allow the US military to use its AI models, the White House described it as "a radical left, woke company" and designated it a supply chain risk, a move that a federal judge has ruled was illegal.

David Sacks, Trump's AI czar in the early days of his administration, has also levelled repeated attacks at Anthropic.

OpenAI has not endured the same level of scrutiny from the White House. When releasing a new model called Astra last week, OpenAI President Greg Brockman described his firm's relationship with the Trump administration as "a very good partnership".

The company did not respond to a BBC inquiry seeking comment.

At the conference in San Francisco this week, the pursuit of fortunes seemed to mostly trump any mounting existential concerns or fears over potential government restrictions on AI.

OpenAI, which was most recently valued at $852bn, has previously announced plans to allow people to buy shares in its firm by listing on the stock market.

However, its chief executive Sam Altman said on Friday this would not happen this year, calling it an "ill-advised moment" to do so "given everything happening with safety" in an interview with Fortune magazine.

He suggested 2027 would be more likely.

Meanwhile, one investor said he was looking forward to Anthropic's forthcoming S-1, a document a company must file with securities regulators in order to sell shares.

His main question about the company was simple: is the firm profitable?

When asked on Thursday if he fears the world may be coming to an end, Sid Sheth - chief executive of the chip company d-Matrix which inked a deal with Nvidia at the conference that day - did not mince his words.

"No," he said.

articles.title: Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI development to slow down
articles.text:
The head of AI company Anthropic has called for the pace of development of artificial intelligence models to slow down and to be closely monitored.

Dario Amodei wrote in an online essay that developing AI was not in question, but that the risks associated with it were "serious" and that companies and governments must be given time to address them.

The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk, have both said they agree with Amodei.

There have been growing concerns recently about the technology's potential risks. An AI researcher who left Anthropic told the BBC that "if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future".

Jacob Coxon told Laura Kuenssberg that people working at AI companies were "genuinely frightened... genuinely concerned about the fate of humanity in the next two years".

"It's not at all an exaggeration to say that the people who are involved with both founding these companies and building the tech believe there is a possibility of human extinction," Coxon said.

In Amodei's essay, called We Must Pace the Frontier and published on Saturday, he proposed a three-point plan that included independent monitoring of AI models as they are developed, industry-wide regulation and global regulation.

As his proposal made the rounds, even competitors voiced support for the idea of third-party monitors who could evaluate the safety of models as they are developed.

"I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier," wrote OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on X. He called independent evaluators "a great idea".

Altman sounded similar safety concerns in a new interview, telling Fortune magazine that standards were "not at a place" to push AI capabilities much further.

He added that he believed AI beyond human control was "absolutely" possible.

Musk, meanwhile, who founded Grok producer xAI, said the Anthropic boss was "right".

The warnings have prompted calls to action, but US President Donald Trump has so far rejected such fears, saying on Thursday he was concerned that "if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position".

Cyber-security concerns have grown as new models have exhibited more and more powerful capabilities.

Anthropic withheld its Mythos model from public use when it was announced in April that it could independently escape the testing environment, known as the sandbox.

In the run-up to the release of its most recent Astra model, OpenAI cited cyber-security concerns as it explained it had paused certain aspects of the model's development.

The OpenAI agents had "essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective", Amodei said. OpenAI has said it was slowing down training of certain advanced AI models and tools as a result.

Safety has also taken centre stage in the rivalry between Anthropic and OpenAI.

Amodei, who had previously worked as a vice-president at OpenAI, has said he co-founded Anthropic in 2021 so he could build safer and more trusted AI models.

He pointed out in his essay that AI had advanced "drastically faster" including its "ability to build the next generation of AI" - and mentioned an incident involving rival OpenAI which has revealed that agents had hacked, external targets they were not asked to attack in July.

Amodei called for "building AI at a balanced rate that aims to ensure its safety while still achieving its benefits".

This would not mean "halting model training or technical progress, but ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models, and for third party evaluators to confirm this".

He was committing Anthropic to this "unilaterally" - as well as calling on governments "to require other frontier companies to match".

Amodei said he recognised that regulation might not be able to keep up with the pace of AI, and therefore called on AI companies to "voluntarily work together to set standard" in parallel with those regulation.

The Anthropic CEO went on to address the impact that a slowdown would have on the industry and competition with leading developers worldwide, particularly China.

"I believe that if slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong," Amodei said.

This would have to be done in a co-ordinated manner "without sacrificing commercial advantage or the United States' lead in AI". Any slowdown would have to be limited, he said, to avoid allowing China to pull ahead.

He urged the US government to take measures so that US companies' AI chips could not be sold to China - or the technology shared with authoritarian countries.

His former employee, Jacob Coxon, told the BBC, however, that the initiative to slow down must go beyond the US - "there'll need to be some sort of co-ordinated slowdown with China if we're going to avoid a race at an international scale".

Amodei's post has prompted a wide range of responses.

Clement Delangue, the CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, said he was launching a new project called the Open Alignment Initiative, adding that he wanted to be among "embedded evaluators" that Amodei proposed could be part of a solution.

Hugging Face was hacked by OpenAI agents earlier this year, prompting outcry over AI safety.

"Let's make AI safer by making it more transparent," Delangue wrote on X.

Musk, who also voices support for Amodei, once called Anthropic "evil" but has changed his tone since signing a $15bn (£11bn) deal to sell computing capacity to Anthropic in May.

However, some observers suggested that Amodei's post was less about safety than about consolidating control over AI technology.

"Dario makes the case to stop open source and concentrate enormous technological and economic power with Anthropic," wrote Chamath Palihapitiya, an investor and co-host of the tech podcast "All-In".

Notions of slowing down or even pausing AI development have long been met with cynicism in certain corners of Silicon Valley, with critics accusing leading AI developers of hyping their technology as a marketing ploy.

Anthropic and OpenAI are both reportedly preparing for potentially record-setting initial public offerings.
