articles.title: Life after Eurovision Song Contest for Ramsgate's Look Mum No Computer
articles.text:
Representing the UK at the Eurovision Song Contest brought Sam Battle one point, but the musician has said the result is a "badge of honour".

Battle, better known by his stage name Look Mum No Computer, represented the UK at this year's Eurovision Song Contest with the electronic pop song Eins, Zwei, Drei.

Looking back on the competition, he said the experience passed in a blur. "It just happened so quick," he said. "I didn't even realise. I was just like, 'oh, I'm jumping on tables, don't fall off the table, Sam, sing'."

He was speaking ahead of his performance on Sunday at the Ramsgate Festival of Sound, external at the Granville Theatre where he plans to include Eins, Zwei, Drei in his set.

Reflecting on finishing at the bottom of the Eurovision scoreboard, Battle said many people had enjoyed the performance.

"I walk around and even a couple of days ago I was walking up to work and a couple of school kids were like, 'you were awesome'," he said.

"It's nice to know that I've made people smile."

Battle grew up in Yaxley, near Peterborough, but has made Ramsgate his home for the past eight years.

"It's great," he said. "I don't see myself going anywhere else."

He spends much of his time at This Museum Is (Not) Obsolete in the Kent town, which houses experimental and obsolete technology.

The museum's collection grew from years spent hunting for bargains at car boot sales and on internet sites.

A Furby organ and a 1960s telephone exchange are among his favourite items.

"You find bargains, you buy the bargains, you end up with loads of bargains and you're a hoarder," he said.

"And then you somehow find yourself in a situation where you can set up a museum and a hoarder is justified as a professional curator."

articles.title: Emily St John Mandel: ‘When half the electorate disagrees on basic reality, how do you come back from that?’
articles.text:
When Emily St John Mandel was a child she had a dream that would stay with her for decades. It was a nightmare in which “I was trying to find my dad in a crowd, and there were other people who looked like him but weren’t him”, she says. “It just kind of struck my imagination.”

Forty-ish years later, Mandel’s seventh novel, Exit Party, opens with a gathering in Los Angeles, 2031, where bizarre things happen. Doubles of some guests appear. Someone else disappears altogether. The novel then alternates between two potential future Americas, one riven by the chaos of civil war, the other a surveillance state.

Doppelgangers and alternative realities are having a cultural moment in our uncanny, deepfake times. Mandel says the biggest challenge western democracy faces is “the collapse of consensual reality. When you get to a situation where half the electorate disagrees on basic reality – for example, who won an election, or is Covid real? I don’t know how you come back from that.” On a more personal level, she has always been fascinated by what she calls “the counter-life – the one where you took a different job or married a different person. The way that, if we made a different decision, we would have become a somewhat different person.”

This interest comes, she thinks, from a feeling that “my life as a writer in New York City is a bit improbable”. Mandel was home-schooled on a tiny island in British Columbia, Canada, before training as a dancer. As she puts it, she was “essentially not educated until I was about 15 … I haven’t got a high school diploma.” She wrote while working office jobs until her third novel, Station Eleven, became a smash hit. The 2014 story of life after a global pandemic felt so prescient when readers rediscovered it during Covid that she developed a reputation for clairvoyance. It has sold 1.5m copies and been translated into 37 languages. Her novels since – The Glass Hotel and Sea of Tranquility – were global bestsellers too. It’s a staggering career, and, as she sees it: “There are a million ways this might not have happened.”

We meet on a sunny New York City day, in the lobby of a sleek Williamsburg hotel. Mandel, who lives in nearby Queens, wears a rose-printed shirt and comes across as warm yet precise. She’s off to have a haircut after we meet, even though her neat pixie cut scarcely looks trimmable.

One of the seeds of Exit Party was its protagonist Ari, who was the villain of Mandel’s second novel, 2010’s The Singer’s Gun. (Mandel is building a multiverse; characters reappear in Station Eleven, The Glass Hotel and Sea of Tranquility, though alas, she says, there is no Marvel movie coming.)

All these years later, “I just couldn’t stop thinking about her. I found myself thinking: what would that character be like at the other end of an 18-year prison sentence?” Ari is like a time traveller, she says; as we all are if we survive enough decades: “If you stick around long enough, you kind of become a migrant from a different timeline.”

Ari is a bit clairvoyant, something Mandel admits – with what I think may be a small wince – is based on her own experience. “I’ve had just a touch of that all my life. A tiny bit. It’s not nearly as useful as you might imagine. I absolutely cannot predict pandemics.” For example, when the March 2020 dates were announced for her Glass Hotel book tour, which was, of course, later cancelled, “I had a strange feeling: I would think about that tour, and it didn’t feel real. The best way I can describe the feeling is to say there was no life in it. When I thought about it, it was inert.” Or she might feel she needs scissors, and bring them to work – and realise she was right. “Dumb little examples like that,” she says, laughing: “Please don’t write that I’m psychic!”

Not psychic, then, but brilliant at imagining what might happen in our disaster-prone world. Even the writing process of this book was eerily predictive – though not in a straightforward way. When Mandel started writing, in spring 2022, she thought the civil war timeline was potentially “our near future. Not to be pessimistic but one reads the news.” Then she came up with an alternative, Universe B, to be “this kind of mirror image – totalitarianism instead of chaos”. By the time the book was nearing completion, with Trump’s bleak second presidency under way, “I felt like I was struggling to stay ahead of the news cycle in Universe B.” Citizens spy on one another and people are disappeared from the streets. “It’s been terrifying to see the speed with which the news cycle has caught up.”

Exit Party is Mandel’s third speculative novel. She is drawn to the form, she says, because she loves to “talk about the present by putting it in a sort of speculative cloak”. Sea of Tranquility, for example, “is absolutely a Covid-19 novel, but by setting it in the future on the moon, it was possible to write about it”. Realism would have been “frankly unbearable to write, let alone to read”. In Exit Party, too, she deftly creates emotional resonance through events that feel like a slanted take on our own times. The titular party, for example, takes place after a curfew is lifted, and has a vividly post-lockdown feel.

Her books come about, she says, through a process of “slow development”. She compares her first draft to a sculptor’s block of clay, “the raw material in which I’ll find the novel. There is no plan and no outline. I’ll start with a scene, build it up from there.” There are always moments when she thinks the novel is irretrievably broken, but she has never yet thrown a manuscript away. “I’ve always been able to change something that isn’t working into something that does work,” she says. Increasingly, she is bringing those skills to the screen, too, whether writing adaptations of her own work (she is working on the pilot for a TV adaptation of Exit Party), or staffing writers’ rooms – recently working on Netflix’s dramatisation of the video game Assassin’s Creed. She spends about one week in Los Angeles for every six in New York, often rising to write fiction in the morning, before an 11am writers’ room Zoom, “which is great in some ways and exhausting in others”.

Mandel recently had her own inflection point. Having divorced from her husband, a fellow writer, in 2022, she married photographer Laura Barisonzi in 2025. Their wedding was the stuff of book nerds’ dreams, held in Brooklyn’s Greenlight book store, which has been “hosting my launch events since before Station Eleven – and I didn’t sell many books back then!” They had an open book bar and her daughter, now 10, was a “ring bearer-slash-flower girl. It was just lovely.”

Exit Party, like much of her work, makes the case for relishing small moments of joy, frightening as the world is. That, she says, is “something I think about a lot. And maybe there’s a way of even appreciating good moments because they’re fleeting. That state of being temporary brings its own kind of sweetness.”

articles.title: ‘You start to worry you’ll never listen to anything else’: 25 years of Can’t Get You Out of My Head, the song that saw the future of pop
articles.text:
Around the release of Pet Shop Boys’ 1988 album Introspective, Neil Tennant coined the term “imperial phase” to describe an era when he felt the duo “understood the essence of pop music and so we felt we could do what we liked”. For his less flowery partner in pop excellence, Chris Lowe, this was typically followed “by disappearing up your backside!”.

In 2010, critic Tom Ewing fleshed out Tennant’s term by imposing three criteria: “command, permission, and self-definition”. Command related to an artist’s willingness and ability to push boundaries in a way that would reverberate through what followed. Permission, meanwhile, connected to the public and their goodwill towards an artist as they pushed things forward. Finally, self-definition, Ewing said, is the way the imperial phase defines the rest of the artist’s career. All future work will be compared with, or mentioned alongside, the output from the imperial phase.

By the time Kylie’s album Fever dropped, everything in its subsequent era represented her very own imperial phase. Everything she did in 2001 and 2002 seemed to click perfectly: every video, every choice of single, the tour, the press attention, the fashion, the cohesiveness of the vision, the way she reshaped pop and nudged it forward. And it was all led by the hypnotic weightlessness of the downright odd Can’t Get You Out of My Head.

The song was born one autumn weekend in 2000 in a garage studio in Surrey belonging to former Mud guitarist Rob Davis, who had been encouraged by manager and impresario Simon Fuller to write some songs with the excellent pop star turned songwriter Cathy Dennis.

On the Sunday, using Cubase on a Mac computer to create a drum loop before adding some guitar, the seed of Can’t Get You Out of My Head was planted. While Dennis came up with the title hook – the song, as she noted, doesn’t really conform to a typical verse-chorus structure, with each line almost acting as its own chorus melody – it was Davis who added the “‘la la la” section. The demo was finished in three hours, while Dennis’s vocals were laid down by 7pm that same day.

The demo was played to Fuller down the phone. He later played it for S Club 7, but they passed on it. The song was also presented to Sophie Ellis-Bextor, but again it was deemed unsuitable. It was Fuller’s idea to send it to Kylie. “And I was thinking: ‘But this song isn’t what Kylie does,’” remembered Dennis. “Obviously, now, none of us knows what Kylie’s going to come out with next, because she can’t be compartmentalised.” Kylie, meanwhile, “knew a few bars in that this was for me”, she wrote in 2002. “By the end of the track I wanted to know how quickly I could get into the studio.”

As promised, though much to Davis’s surprise given he’d convinced himself she wouldn’t turn up, Kylie arrived in Surrey to record Can’t Get You Out of My Head. In between some fancy salmon salad and other treats, the song was finished in a few hours. The mysterious pop alchemy of adding Kylie to a song took them all by surprise. “Even though Kylie wasn’t the first artist to be offered the song, I don’t believe it was meant to go to anyone other than Kylie,” said Dennis,“and I don’t believe anyone else would have done the incredible job she did with it, with the video, looking super-hot!”

Can’t Get You Out of My Head wasn’t just “good, for a pop song”, as joyless people were wont to say, keen to use the caveat in case their muso credentials be tarnished. As pop began to absorb the outre production styles of R&B experimentalists such as the Neptunes and Timbaland – Britney’s career-restructuring I’m a Slave 4 U, produced by the former, would arrive in the same month as Can’t Get You Out of My Head – audiences were becoming more attuned to pop that was looking to push the boundaries. This felt like dance-pop beamed in from the future, where the first time you hear it you’re like, “Huh?” then the second you’re like, “Wait!” and then the 35th time you start to worry you may never listen to anything else.

Its title becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. Can’t Get You Out of My Head’s sexy futurism would also dictate the visual feel of the era: sleek lines, icy-cool silhouettes and just a hint of something darker lurking underneath. For the album’s cover, shot by Vincent Peters, Kylie’s stylist and creative director William Baker was inspired by the French artist Jean-Paul Goude’s photos of Grace Jones, which highlighted both her sexuality and her power. Baker also wanted Kylie to be attached to the tools of her trade, so on both the album cover and artwork for Can’t Get You Out of My Head, a microphone’s black power cord winds its way round Kylie’s body.

Less overt than the buttock-hugging, Carry On vibes of Kylie’s previous album, Light Years, and its lead single, Spinning Around, the Fever look was leaning more into an artful sexiness. This was highlighted in Can’t Get You Out of My Head’s video, directed by Dawn Shadforth, in which the utopia promised by the millennium was laid out in front of us via forensically manicured cityscapes and futuristic fashion: we see her dance on what looks like a rooftop garden centre and in a clean white dome, and losing herself in a dress made of purple-silver Post-it notes.

It also gave Kylie yet another iconic fashion moment, one that would be replicated at gigs and fancy-dress parties for decades to come, in the shape of the white hooded dress, split to the navel.

While the dress grabbed the attention, it was the all-in-red dancers behind Kylie, sporting matching face-covering visors, who caused a problem for Top of the Pops producer Chris Cowey. As Can’t Get You Out of My Head started to dominate, the show’s lighting department began to complain that their red gels were going missing at the show’s on-set afterparty “because everyone was taking [them] and wrapping them around their heads and doing the dance”, Cowey says. “Just kind of drunkenly doing Kylie impersonations.”

By the early 2000s, after Oasis v Blur, the UK had become mildly obsessed with chart battles, ideally those featuring attractive women. On 17 September 2001, the same day as Can’t Get You Out of My Head, Victoria “Posh Spice” Beckham was set to release Not Such an Innocent Girl, the lead single from her self-titled debut solo album.

Posh had already been beaten, the previous year, by actually-quite-posh Sophie Ellis-Bextor, whose Rob Davis-assisted Groovejet (If This Ain’t Love) had left Beckham’s banger Out of Your Mind at No 2. This time, Victoria roared on to the battlefield with a ropey single and mildly scathing bons mots for her Australian rival. “When I first heard [Can’t Get You Out of My Head], if I’m being totally honest, I didn’t like it,” Posh mused. “And I’m being completely honest.”

For Posh, “an old-fashioned type songwriter”, Kylie’s single, while having “a very catchy melody”, didn’t resonate with her because she enjoys “a song that has a bit of emotion”. Posh was also retroactively blaming Kylie for criticisms of Out of Your Mind: “And I have to say that last year when I brought out a dance record, and I had effects on my voice, like she has on her voice, I am still getting a caning for it now.”

In the end, on the UK chart of 23 September, Can’t Get You Out of My Head crashed in at No 1, shifting an eye-watering 306,000 copies, holding off emerging talent Bob the Builder’s cover of Mambo No 5 in the process. It would stay at No 1 in the UK for a month, a feat matched in Australia. Posh’s Not Such an Innocent Girl would have to make do with a No 6 entry in the UK and sales of 35,000. The clash was such a hot topic that the BBC ran a news story with the headline: Kylie trounces Posh in chart battle. “Victoria is pleased to have a Top 10 hit,” a Posh spokeswoman was quoted as saying.

This particular pop star chart battle also served a specific escapist aim. Both singles were released shortly after 9/11, as the western world tried to recalibrate itself following a terrorist attack. The horrors seemed so overwhelming that any hint of normality was gripped tightly with both hands, and Can’t Get You Out of My Head’s futuristic escapism became a hypnotic balm.

For some journalists, the mere existence of Kylie was proof that Osama bin Laden and the Taliban could never win the “war on terror”. “Two people dominated the cultural landscape of this country in the last quarter of the year: Osama bin Laden and Kylie Minogue,” wrote Julie Burchill in the Guardian as 2001 came to an end. “I really do believe that Bin Laden and Kylie represent the polar opposites of human nature; the first all about cruelty without beauty, the second all about beauty without cruelty.”

Kylie was suddenly being held up as an emblem of western ideals – the literal face (and body) of the UK’s reaction to the global threat from a terrorist organisation. The Daily Mail printed a list of reasons to be cheerful, post-9/11, topped by Kylie. The picture they used alongside the piece was captioned “Fungirl Kylie, scourge of the Taliban”. Watching from the outside as this narrative unfolded, Kylie was “dumbfounded. I understand the way they’re seeing it as a positive thing, but no! Don’t write things like that!”

Actual human Kylie, not the projected superhero being pushed to the frontlines, was being interviewed live on local radio when the attacks took place. One of the DJs asked her on air, “So how does it feel to be a pop star in this situation?” “A two-second silence on live radio seems for ever,” Kylie remembered in the Face magazine. “I said: ‘I can’t believe you just asked me that.’ I think they swiftly cut to a record.”

Americans, at first, clung to a very different kind of superstar and song. Enrique Iglesias’s windswept ballad Hero, released on 3 September 2001, was one of the few songs played by New York City DJs after the attacks, but by the time Can’t Get You Out of My Head made its debut on the US charts in January 2002, a shift was happening. People needed something to dance to. “It was definitely at a time when people were gingerly going back [out],” remembers NYC music journalist Larry Flick. “I think [Can’t Get You Out of My Head] came at a time when we just needed Kylie, and an artist that wasn’t going to take it all too seriously. There were a few things, in New York, that got us through 9/11: there was the return of Friends, the return of David Letterman, and the Kylie record.”

Flick remembers the second time he heard it, in the Roxy, New York’s disco roller rink turned hip nightclub, which was famed as a venue that tested out new records. “I ran to the booth and I was like: ‘How about you playing Kylie?’ And the DJ goes: ‘Baby, this is the shit.’ He played it for about 20 minutes and the crowd lost their minds.”

Can’t Get You Out of My Head wasn’t just a hit; it was a smash. It didn’t just peak in all the usual places Kylie tended to, but also in places such as Belgium and Romania and Switzerland and Hungary. In the US, it quickly started to climb not just the Dance Club charts, where Kylie had been a regular, but also the main Billboard Hot 100, a chart she hadn’t been in since 1988.

“Can’t Get You Out of My Head was inescapable,” remembers US Kylie fan David Russell. “It started to get played on the radio, and then suddenly the video was on MTV. Kylie did Saturday Night Live with Ian McKellen hosting. I begged the publicist and she got me in. McKellen said: ‘You lucky, lucky people, it’s Kylie Minogue!’ He then sat on the side of the stage like a little kid watching her.”

Back in the UK, Kylie won twice at the 2002 Brit awards, scooping best international female and best international album for Fever. But it was her award-show performance that would gain instant notoriety, later becoming a mainstay of any homosexual’s post-night-out YouTube binge.

Performing a special mashup of Can’t Get You Out of My Head and New Order’s Blue Monday by then white-hot DJ and producer Erol Alkan, whose Trash club night was London’s hottest ticket, Kylie arrives on stage lying down on a giant CD – her name emblazoned on it in neon pink – seemingly holding on for dear life while wearing a Dolce & Gabbana minidress and knee-high silver boots. As the giant CD is ejected out of the player and lifts up so the crowd can see her for the first time, you’ll believe you can hear God. The performance was a perfect balancing act: audacious, spectacular, camp, sexy and silly in all the right ways.

“I feel like I’m on a wave and I actually know how to stand on the board at this point,” Kylie said as Can’t Get You Out of My Head and her imperial era kicked in. “I don’t know where it’s taking me, but everything feels really good.”

articles.title: Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom review – Aardman’s spooky-season caper sparkles with fun
articles.text:
Summer is over and Halloween is on the way … not for a fair bit, of course, but if all the UK’s Halloween merch and continuing pop culture content is up to the standard of this film, then no one is going to be complaining. This is the third in Aardman’s thoroughly enjoyable and cleverly written Shaun the Sheep stop-motion franchise of what are effectively silent movies, with a few intelligible words. It is the story of gutsy and heroic sheep involved in amazing adventures in the sleepy village of Mossy Bottom, starring characters who first appeared in the Wallace and Gromit short film A Close Shave.

This one is another excellent family film, crammed as ever with top visual gags, great throwaway references and, of course, a homemade Heath Robinson contraption, so often to be found in Aardman films. We get nods to The Archers, The Wombles and The Simpsons; there’s a wacky chase worthy of What’s Up, Doc?; a homage to the notorious waxing scene from Judd Apatow’s The 40-Year-Old Virgin; and even what appears to be a brief visual walk-on for George Bernard Shaw as Bigfoot. As ever with Shaun the Sheep and Aardman Animations generally, the standard of writing is extremely high and the script here, from Mark Burton and Giles Pilbrow, sparkles with good-natured fun. One high-street hairdressing salon in the wool-producing district where it’s set is called Barber Black Sheep – and if no real-life shop has stolen this joke yet, they ought to.

A klutzy, balding sheep farmer (voiced by John Sparkes), on whose premises Shaun and the gang are to be found, is poignantly in love with a visiting vet (voiced by Nina Sosanya); he longs to invite her to a local country music hoedown, but is shy and moreover ashamed of being follicularly challenged. As for the sheep themselves, they are secretly cultivating a pumpkin patch to harvest a bunch of scary jack-o-lanterns for their forthcoming Halloween frolics. The clumsy big-booted farmer ruins them all, and the resourceful sheep turn to the dark magic of technology and sinister GM techniques (as discovered in a children’s science book) to grow supersized new pumpkins from a rescued seed. But some of their occult new miracle growth-boost liquid finds its way into the farmer’s baldness-cure bottle.

The pitchfork-wielding villagers of Mossy Bottom are hilariously stunned at the terrifying appearance of a rampaging, hairy beast who has been spotted in the outlying fields and woodlands at the very moment that the farmer himself has mysteriously disappeared. Has the beast somehow kidnapped or eaten the farmer? It is a nightmarish mystery that will need every ounce of Shaun and his pals’ courage and ingenuity to sort out, not to mention that of the vet, who uses a hi-tech DNA machine to examine the genetic provenance of a piece of the beast’s fur she has managed to snip off.

It is a love story of sorts, perhaps a little like that of Beauty and the Beast, but about two people who for most the story’s running time don’t know that they are going to be in love. As for the sheep, their faces convey amazingly distinct expressions and moods with just a few deft movements. It’s sharp, smart, funny and precise; there is nothing woolly about it.

Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom is out on 17 September in Australia, and on 18 September in the UK and US.
